    #136981. Has That Final Destination Truck Scene Ever Actually Happened in Real Life?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (798 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Familyhandyman ↗ Open Full Page

    Has That Final Destination Truck Scene Ever Actually Happened in Real Life?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here's what real-world crash data actually states about the likelihood of a Final Destination truck scene.
    • According to recent reports, giving drivers a reason to fear logging trucks since 2003, Final Destination 2 opened with one of the franchise’s most visceral—and memorable—scenes.
    • Yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Here's what real-world crash data actually states about the likelihood of a Final Destination truck scene.

    According to recent reports, giving drivers a reason to fear logging trucks since 2003, Final Destination 2 opened with one of the franchise’s most visceral—and memorable—scenes. A logging truck traveling down a busy highway spills its cargo and sets off a chain reaction of intense car crashes. It’s a gruesome, cinematic disaster, but the basic danger is grounded in reality. Logs can come loose during transport, with serious consequences on a busy road. Has anything like the Final Destination truck scene actually happened in real life?

    Yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents. However, the Final Destination truck scene depicting this realistic road hazard is grossly exaggerated. Logs can fall off of trucks and cause accidents, but they don’t bounce down the highway and become windshield-level projectiles like in the film. So, yes, the danger is real, but the chain-reaction chaos depicted in the film is highly dramatized.

    In a recent development, in January 2024, a logging truck on Interstate 95 in Florida overturned while traveling too fast through a curve in the road. Logs spilled onto the highway, rolled over a barrier and into oncoming traffic. A Jacksonville man who was involved in the accident told local reporters, “I just had a real life Final Destination moment…” However, he and all other motorists were unharmed. In June of 2025, another turnover dumped not logs, but large metal pipes across Highway 75 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, closing both lanes of traffic. Again, no injuries were reported. A fatal accident involving a logging truck did occur in Arkansas in 2014. While traveling down Highway 65, the truck blew a rear tire, swerved into a bridge construction site and tipped over. Two construction workers were killed by the discharged logs.

    Each year, shifting or unsecured loads carried by commercial vehicles are linked to roughly 4,000 to 7,000 accidents. This may not sound like a lot, but these accidents have severe consequences, often resulting in serious injury or death. “They regularly make news headlines, so the average person may think they’re more common than they are,” personal injury attorney Juan Dominguez says. In fact, the most dangerous vehicles carrying cargo are non-commercial cars and trucks. 73 percent of highway accidents involving road debris are caused by passenger vehicles with unsecured loads. Commercial trucks are closely regulated and inspected for proper load security, contributing to lower accident rates. Despite the attention given to logging truck accidents, they are only involved in 1.5 percent of all fatal commercial truck accidents each year.

    Industry observers note that take control of your safety when sharing the road with large cargo trucks. Here’s how:.

    Sources indicate that “My first rule is to never drive directly behind a truck with a [loose] load like logs, pipes or steel beams,” construction safety specialist Steven Menotti notes. “If the load shifts or falls off, you’ll be the first vehicle it hits.” If you have to drive behind a cargo truck,  increase your following distance to at least four seconds, which allows for more reaction time if debris falls into the road. “That distance can help if the unexpected happens and something comes loose,” Dominguez says. “You have more time to try and react.” If possible, reduce your speed for a shorter stopping distance.

    Recent findings suggest that if you need to pass a truck on the highway, time it so you can rapidly complete the pass and return to the lane. Avoid driving directly next to a cargo truck for an extended length of time to avoid being hit by falling debris or cargo.

    If you spot a truck without a properly secured load, move away from it on the road. Look for worn or loose straps and chains, unevenly loaded cargo or missing side stakes. “Those all indicate the trucker probably didn’t check the load,” Menotti states. “I won’t follow it. I change lanes, and pull far back.”.

    Logs can fall from trucks, but they don’t bounce or become projectiles across the highway like the Final Destination truck scene. In the film, this depiction was CGI-generated.

    Brake hard and avoid swerving. Swerving causes 37 percent of all road debris accident fatalities, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

    American Automobile Association: American Drivers Aren’t Securing Loads (2016).

    #136980. Tech Report: Further Discussion of Whether Current Second Amendment Jurisprudence Is Based on a "Misquote"

    Tech Report: Further Discussion of Whether Current Second Amendment Jurisprudence Is Based on a "Misquote"

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (487 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Reason

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I recently appeared on an episode of the Reload podcast, hosted by Reload founder and editor Stephen Gutowski, to discuss my blog post taking aim at the Fresh York Times story alleging current Second Amendment jurisprudence is based upon a "misquote" of Blackstone.
    • As noted in my original post, the NYT story was harshly criticized by attorney John Bash, a former clerk to Justice Scalia during the term Heller was decided who was interviewed (but not quoted) in the story.
    • As I note on the podcast, there are perfectly reasonable arguments that current Second Amendment jurisprudence has gone astray, and that some courts have placed undue weight on the contested passage in the Heller opinion (which did not purport to set out a test).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I recently appeared on an episode of the Reload podcast, hosted by Reload founder and editor Stephen Gutowski, to discuss my blog post taking aim at the Fresh York Times story alleging current Second Amendment jurisprudence is based upon a "misquote" of Blackstone.

    As noted in my original post, the NYT story was harshly criticized by attorney John Bash, a former clerk to Justice Scalia during the term Heller was decided who was interviewed (but not quoted) in the story. As also noted in that post, the Times issued a response to my post. As discussed in the podcast, I did not find the response particularly persuasive, nor did John Bash.

    As I note on the podcast, there are perfectly reasonable arguments that current Second Amendment jurisprudence has gone astray, and that some courts have placed undue weight on the contested passage in the Heller opinion (which did not purport to set out a test). But these are separate questions from whether there was a "misquote" in the Heller opinion. It seems to me the obsession with the latter derives from a desire to discredit contemporary gun rights jurisprudence by suggesting it all stems from a mistake (or worse), rather than by contesting it on the merits.

    As for the Blackstone source at issue, just as the Times did not place the contested Heller passage in its full context so that readers could see the point Scalia was making, it did not highlight the full Blackstone passage (other than providing a hyperlink in the web version of the story) or unpack the point Blackstone was making--a point that is arguably even less favorable to gun ownership restrictions than is the relevant passage in Heller.

    in his seminal 1769 treatise, "Commentaries on the Laws of England," Blackstone referred to weapons that were "dangerous or unusual," suggesting that a gun did not need to be both in order to be restricted.

    The offence of riding or going armed, with dangerous or unusual weapons, is a crime against the public peace, by terrifying the good people of the land; and is particularly prohibited by the statute of Northampton, upon pair of forfeiture of the arms, and imprisonment during the king's pleasure: in like manner as, by the laws of Solon, every Athenian was finable who walked about the city in armour.

    Those who want gun rights jurisprudence to hew more closely to Blackstone than does Heller want to be careful what they wish for, as it might not be much authority at all for laws prohibiting the mere possession of unusually dangerous weapons (such as those the Supreme Court will consider this term), as opposed to laws prohibiting the carrying of such arms in ways that could "terrify[]." The Times does not "misquote" Blackstone, but some might conclude the Times was not fairly representing what Blackstone wrote either.

    Sources indicate that when we started researching the best power strips, we discovered hundreds of different options on the market, so we started by looking carefully at the top-rated models.     Since the primary purpose of buying a power strip is to have additional outlets, we noted how easy (or difficult) it was to use all of the outlets on the strip at the same time. Our goal wasn’t to see how much power we could pull—that depends solely on the circuit—but to see how well the strips were designed for real-world use.

    We awarded points based on a rubric: the better a strip performed on a test or assessment, the higher the points. After testing, we averaged the points to find our top pick and categorize the others by their best use.

    Before choosing the best power strip for your needs, consider how and where you proposal to use it, as well as the notable factors below.

    The right power strip for your needs depends heavily on how it will be used and which devices or equipment will be plugged into it.

    It has been revealed that the number of outlets you need in a power strip depends on both how many and what type of devices you want to plug into it. Remember that you should not plug high-power-capacity devices into power strips, regardless of the number of outlets. The circuit still limits the power strip.

    Power strips can have as few as two outlets or more than 20. These outlets can be standard power outlets, USB-A or USB-C outlets, wide-spaced outlets intended for larger adapters, and specialty connections like ethernet or coaxial connections. The number and configuration of outlets are mostly a personal preference; however, consider that as the number of outlets increases, so does the size of the power strip. So, if space is an matter, choose a power strip with fewer outlets and a narrower profile.

    Length and configuration refer to the length of the cord and the type of outlets in the power strip.

    In our technologically advanced society, many devices and appliances embedded with complex electrical systems are very sensitive to power surges, so surge protection is a feature of a power strip nearly everyone needs. Power surges typically occur when a storm brings down electrical lines, causing the power company to reroute power to address power demands. These changes can create inconsistent power flow fluctuations, resulting in a power surge. The only way to protect all appliances and devices is with a whole-house surge protector, but strips with surge protection will reduce the risk of damage to sensitive electronics and devices.

    Sources indicate that surge protection—also referred to as the surge suppression rating of a power strip—is measured in joules (J) and normally varies, depending on the product, from as low as 100 J to higher than 4,000 J. When using a power strip as surge protection for expensive or sensitive devices, it is key to invest in a power strip with a high surge suppression rating.

    Recent findings suggest that A standard power strip runs electricity to multiple devices, typically via an on/off switch. Smart power strips function similarly, but they can also connect with compatible smart home systems, like Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant, usually through a WiFi connection.

    Industry observers note that once a smart power strip connects to a smart home system, users can control the electrical supply to the paired devices through either voice control or a smartphone app. Some power strips even support timers or schedules so connected devices will automatically turn on or off.

    It has been revealed that while power strips don’t seem very dangerous, cords can become trip hazards and electrocution and fires can result from improper use. Many power strip manufacturers include safety features like full-metal housing, internal circuit breakers, or ground-fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs) to protect owners and their property from harm.

    Take a look below to find the answers to some of the most commonly asked questions about electrical power outlet strips.

    If used properly, a power strip can actually reduce the risk of electrical fire by providing a safe place to plug in additional accessories. However, if misused, either by overloading it, using it for appliances it’s not rated for, or linking multiple power strips together (called daisy-chaining), a power strip can become a danger.

    Never plug high-power-capacity appliances, such as electric space heaters, refrigerators, microwaves, toaster ovens, and air conditioners, into a power strip.

    In a recent development, daisy-chaining power strips means linking multiple power strips together in a series that connects back to a single electrical outlet. This is a big concern for fire-fighting professionals because daisy-chained connections will almost invariably lead to an overloaded power strip that heats up until it burns out or catches fire.

    Power strips can catch fire if they are old or frayed, or if they are overloaded beyond their capacity. This can happen when several devices that draw too much electricity, such as air conditioners or electric heaters, are plugged into the same strip. The strip will then heat up and eventually begin to melt, sparking a fire.

    In a recent development, while there is some discrepancy between specific products, on average, power strips will last for about 2 years before replacement is necessary. However, they can last between 3 to 5 years if properly maintained.

    In a recent development, it depends on what you plug into the strips, but in general, it’s not a good practice to plug two strips into one outlet. Overloading the circuit will cause the breaker to trip.

    Sources indicate that in a home that has too few outlets for the owners’ needs, power strips can absolutely be worth the money because they expand the number of outlets available. Power strips that have surge protection are also ideal for homes with a lot of sensitive electronics, as the strips prevent damage when power surges might otherwise cause damage. Just keep in mind that power strips don’t actually provide more power to the home—they just allow more devices to use the power that’s already there.

    It’s not a bad idea. Turning it off will reduce standby energy usage, but as long as you’re not overloading the circuit, it should be safe to leave on.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Give your coffee maker a home with this coffee station organizer.
    • Industry observers note that our editors and experts handpick every product we feature.
    • Clear the counter clutter and fuel your mornings with a scrap-wood coffee station that has a spot for everything.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Give your coffee maker a home with this coffee station organizer.

    Industry observers note that our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

    Clear the counter clutter and fuel your mornings with a scrap-wood coffee station that has a spot for everything.

    According to recent reports, if you know three things about me, it’s that I’m a stickler for organization, I run on coffee, and I can’t throw away wood scraps. This coffee station checks all three boxes.

    It’s built almost entirely from maple offcuts, which explains the mix of thicknesses on the Cutting List. To keep it approachable, every joint is a simple butt joint with glue and brad nails. Biscuits are used only for the glued-up panels. If you can make square cuts and run a nailer, you can build this in a weekend.

    [Please insert TA “Coffee_org_case.pdf” here with callouts.].

    [Please insert TA “Coffee_org_drawer.pdf” here with callouts.].

    Boards wide enough for the top (A) and base (B) are almost impossible to find, so I made the panels by joining several boards with biscuits.

    Recent findings suggest that cut the boards at least 1/2-in. longer and wider than needed. The extra material lets you trim the panels square and to size after the glue dries.

    Industry observers note that mark across each joint where you want a biscuit, spacing them 6- to 8-in. apart and about 3-in. from each end. Cut the slots with a biscuit joiner. Be generous with the glue in the slots and along the edges. You want an even bead of squeeze-out so you know you have good coverage. Clamp the panels and keep them flat as they dry.

    Industry observers note that once the glue dries, scrape off the squeeze-out and cut the top (A) and base (B) to the final size. Then cut the rest of the parts following the cutting list.

    Connect the two sides (C) and the back (E) to the base (B) of the coffee organizer using 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Secure the sides so they’re flush with the bottom of the base. Set the back on the base between the sides, flush with the back edges of the base (B) and sides (C).

    Sources indicate that cut the pieces for the butcher block (L) and biscuit-join them the same way you did the panels. Again, cut them at least 1/2-in. oversize. That allows for the wood shifting during clamping and leaves enough on each end to make clean, square cuts once the glue has dried.

    Recent findings suggest that once the glue is dry, cut the butcher block to final size on the table saw. Scrape and sand off the dried glue, then round over the sharp edges with a router and a bearing-guided 1/4-in. round-over bit.

    It has been revealed that when you size the butcher block, leave room for the drawer slides you’ll install later. Most need about 1/2-in. on each side, so a 13-in. opening takes a 12-in.-wide butcher block.

    According to recent reports, the left-hand compartment houses the butcher block and drawer, so it needs to be 13-in. wide: 12-in. for the butcher block and drawer, plus 1-in. for the drawer slides. Mark the divider location, then test-fit the butcher block and loose drawer slides to confirm the opening. Apply glue and secure the center divider (D) with 18-gauge brad nails driven up through the base (B) and in through the back (E).

    Sources indicate that note: Drawer slide clearance varies by style and manufacturer. Check your slides’ specs and adjust the opening as needed.

    According to recent reports, build a drawer to store coffee pods and spoons. Glue and nail the drawer box front and back (G) to the ends of the sides (F), then attach the bottom (H) to square it up. The drawer front (K) covers the nails on the front.

    It has been revealed that secure the drawer dividers (J) inside the drawer (Fig. B) with wood glue and brad nails, spacing them to fit your coffee pods, spoons, or other items. Feel free to add or take away dividers as needed. I left 1-1/2-in.-wide slots for pods and a 4-in.-wide slot for spoons.

    On the left side of the coffee organizer, install the butcher block (L) and drawer using your drawer slides and the included hardware. Both attach to the left side (C) and center divider (D), so install the butcher block first and the drawer above it. Pre-drill and hand-screw for proper alignment and to avoid stripping the screws.

    Sources indicate that once the butcher block (L) and drawer are installed, cover the left compartment with the top (A), securing it with glue and 18-gauge brad nails. The right side stays open.

    Then attach the drawer front (K) to the drawer box front so it overlaps the left side (C) and center divider (D). Use double-sided tape to position it and 1-in. screws from inside the drawer box to lock it down.

    In a recent development, install and secure dividers on the right side of the unit with 1-1/4-inch 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Working from the front to the back of the coffee station:.

    In a recent development, in the 6-1/4-in. space between the front face (M) and the short divider (N), install the tea separators (R) and spacers (S and T) to make a divided area for sugar, teas, stirrers, etc. Use a 23-gauge nailer and 5/8-in. nails to secure the spacers (S and T) to the front face (M) and short divider (N), then slide the tea separators (R) into the gaps between them. My compartments were 2-1/8-in. and 3-in. wide, but feel free to make them whatever size you’d like.

    Industry observers note that sink any protruding nails, fill the nail holes with wood filler, and finish-sand the entire piece. Apply a finish to the whole unit. I used Tried & True Original Wood Finish, which is food-safe, so it works on the butcher block and everything else.

    Sources indicate that then install the handles on the drawer and butcher block. You can’t reach behind the solid butcher block to drive a screw, so cut the head off the handle screw with a hacksaw, drill a pilot hole, and glue the cut end into it with CA glue or epoxy.

    A food-safe wood finish won’t transfer chemicals or toxins to the food when being used. There are two ways a finish is considered food-safe. Either it is completely non-toxic and edible in its liquid state from its origin, or, once fully cured, the VOCs (volatile organic compounds) in the finish disperse, and it becomes a stable, inert, non-toxic solid. Finishes like food-grade mineral oil or fractionated coconut oil are considered food-safe from the time of application and work well as food-safe wood finishes.

    A coffee station should include options for coffee or tea, sweeteners, flavoring and stirring. Focus on organization and easy access tiers – no matter what you choose to present in your coffee station.

    42-in. works well for a free-standing coffee station cabinet. This is slightly higher than a standard 36-in. countertop height and lower than a 45-in. bar height top. For a coffee station on a countertop beneath upper cabinets, you want enough clearance to open and close your coffee maker’s lid. A 6-in. tall coffee station would give you 12-in. clearance in a standard 18-in. opening between the top of the counter and the bottom of the upper cabinets.

    Although the public has a substantial interest in protecting freedom of expression, it also has an interest in protecting individuals against reputational injury caused by defamatory falsehoods.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Industry observers note that A Christmas tree may explain those December sniffles. Learn what Christmas tree syndrome feels like and how to reduce common triggers at home.

    Recent findings suggest that being at home during the holidays can be a magical time of year for many. But for some, it also means dealing with allergies. Christmas tree syndrome could be responsible. Sneezing might start soon after the Christmas decorations go up, sometimes happening around the same time every year.

    Dr. Racheal Onah, ND, consulting physician with RealTime Labs, explains what causes it, which symptoms to watch for, and how families can reduce their exposure.

    In a recent development, christmas tree syndrome refers to allergy and asthma symptoms that appear after putting up a Christmas tree or holiday decorations. Onah explains that the term is a nickname, not an official diagnosis, though the reactions are real.

    Real Christmas trees can bring mold, pollen, and other allergens into the house. A study published in the Annals of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology identified several types of mold on Christmas trees, including some that can cause allergies.

    Recent findings suggest that “Outdoors, molds play a part in nature by breaking down dead organic matter such as fallen leaves and dead trees, but indoors, mold growth should be avoided,” explains the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. “Molds reproduce by means of tiny spores; the spores are invisible to the naked eye and float through outdoor and indoor air.”.

    Symptoms can include, but are not limited to:.

    Symptoms that get worse around the tree but improve away from home may point to an allergy. Onah notes frequent sneezing and itchy eyes without a fever suggest an allergic reaction rather than a virus. A cold is more likely to bring a fever, sore throat, or body aches.

    In a recent development, onah suggests checking for mold or musty smells before buying a real tree. She recommends having the tree lot shake off loose debris, then rinsing the tree outside and letting it dry before bringing it indoors. Once inside, Onah recommends keeping the tree away from heating vents and running a HEPA air purifier in the same room.

    Iuliia Burmistrova/Getty Images.

    Artificial trees can cause problems, too, depending on where and how they’re stored.

    “Artificial trees that sat in a garage or basement for 11 months have had plenty of time to collect dust and moisture,” indicates Onah. “They are often stored in the original cardboard boxes they came in, which is a material that holds onto humidity and can feed mold on its own.”.

    According to recent reports, wreaths, garlands, and fabric decorations can collect dust or develop mold in storage as well. Scented candles and artificial snow sprays may also bother people with allergies.

    It has been revealed that onah recommends unpacking decorations outside and wiping down artificial branches before setting them up. She notes glass, metal, and hard plastic ornaments can be washed with warm water and mild dish soap. Porous decorations with visible mold or a musty smell, such as fabric, paper, or wood pieces, should be thrown away.

    It has been revealed that “When the season is over, make sure everything is completely dry before you pack it away,” states Onah. “Use sealed plastic bins instead of cardboard, add a few silica gel packets to absorb moisture, and store everything off the floor. If possible, opt to store your bins in a climate-controlled space like an interior closet rather than a garage, attic or basement.”.

    Anyone dealing with recurring allergy symptoms or worsening asthma should check with a healthcare provider.

    Recent findings suggest that “I’d pay extra attention if symptoms linger after the decorations come down,” notes Onah. “This could be a sign the decor stirred up a bigger mold problem in the home, like a damp storage area or an HVAC system that’s harboring growth.”.

    The lawsuit was filed in September, but the Justice Department press release just showed up on Westlaw a couple of days ago. Here's what the Supreme Court said about licensing fees in Bruen:.

    To be clear, nothing in our analysis should be interpreted to suggest the unconstitutionality of the 43 States' "shall-matter" licensing regimes, under which "a general desire for self-defense is sufficient to obtain a [permit]." Because these licensing regimes do not require applicants to show an atypical need for armed self-defense, they do not necessarily prevent "law-abiding, responsible citizens" from exercising their Second Amendment right to public carry.

    Rather, it appears that these shall-problem regimes, which often require applicants to undergo a background check or pass a firearms safety course, are designed to ensure only that those bearing arms in the jurisdiction are, in fact, "law-abiding, responsible citizens." And they likewise appear to contain only "narrow, objective, and definite standards" guiding licensing officials, rather than requiring the "appraisal of facts, the exercise of judgment, and the formation of an opinion"—features that typify proper-cause standards like Newly introduced York's.

    That mentioned, because any permitting scheme can be put toward abusive ends, we do not rule out constitutional challenges to shall-issue regimes where, for example, lengthy wait times in processing license applications or exorbitant fees deny ordinary citizens their right to public carry.

    $1591, a fee that is nearly seven times the cost of a newly introduced inexpensive handgun, strikes me as pretty exorbitant.

    Note that there is no categorical constitutional rule banning fees for the exercise of constitutional rights. Taxes based on the content of speech are generally unconstitutional, regardless of their magnitude. But this is a special case of the principle that discrimination based on certain kinds of characteristics—race, sex, religiosity, or the content or viewpoint of speech—is unconstitutional.

    Setting aside these special areas of constitutionally forbidden discrimination, and setting aside poll taxes, which were constitutional until the Twenty-Fourth Amendment forbade them, other kinds of taxes, fees, and indirect costs imposed on the exercise of constitutional rights are often permissible. The government may require modest content-neutral fees for demonstration permits or charitable fundraising permits, at least if the fees are tailored to defraying the costs of administering constitutionally permissible regulatory regimes. The same is true for marriage license fees and filing fees for political candidates (though the Court has held that the right to run for office is in some measure protected by the First Amendment). The same is doubtlessly true of costs involved in getting permits to build on your own property, a right protected by the Takings Clause.

    According to recent reports, likewise, when the Court recognized a right to abortion, abortion regulations were not rendered unconstitutional simply because they increase the cost of an abortion. The Court so held when upholding a 24-hour waiting period even though it required some women in states with very few abortion providers to stay in a hotel overnight or miss a day of work, and when upholding viability testing requirements that might have marginally increased the cost of an abortion. So long as the extra costs don't amount to "substantial obstacle[s]" to a woman's getting an abortion, they are constitutional.

    At the same time, when a cost is high enough to impose a substantial obstacle to the exercise of a right for a considerable number of people, it is unconstitutional; and I think that's true of the nearly $1600 fee charged by San Jose. This is likely also true when a cost goes materially beyond the cost of administering the otherwise permissible regulatory scheme. And if a law substantially burdens rightholders who are relatively poor, an exemption would likely be constitutionally required.

    For more on this, see the footnotes on pp. 1543-44 of my Implementing the Right to Keep and Bear Arms in Self-Defense article.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Plaintiffs … filed this action against the United States, Google LLC ("Google"), and X.AI Corp.
    • Plaintiffs allege that in "late 2025 and early 2026, the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that from Magistrate Judge Virginia DeMarchi (N.D. Cal.) today in Doe 1 v. U.S.:.

    Plaintiffs … filed this action against the United States, Google LLC ("Google"), and X.AI Corp. ("X.AI"). Plaintiffs sue for themselves and on behalf of a proposed class of "[a]ll Jeffrey Epstein victims whose private information, including their name, photographic image, telephone number, email address, physical address, or place of residence, was disclosed without their consent in unredacted documents released by the United States between December 2025 and the present." Plaintiffs also sue on behalf of an injunctive relief subclass of "[a]ll Class members whose disclosed private information is indexed, cached, hosted, or otherwise made available to the public through any service operated by the United States, Google, or [X.AI]." The subclass "seeks injunctive relief under Rules 23(b)(2) only.".

    Plaintiffs allege that in "late 2025 and early 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice ('DOJ') outed approximately 100 victims of the convicted sexual predator, publishing their private information and identifying them to the world." Plaintiffs further allege that "[e]ven after the government acknowledged the disclosure violated the rights of the victims and withdrew most of the information, artificial intelligence products like Google's AI Mode and [X.]AI's Grok, continue to republish it, refusing victims' pleas to take it down." Plaintiffs' sole claim against the United States is for violation of the Privacy Act of 1974 ("Privacy Act"), 5 U.S.C. § 552a(b) and § 552(g)(1)(D). Plaintiffs assert several claims under California law and common law against both Google and X.AI for violation of California's Unfair Competition Law (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200, et seq.), invasion of privacy, negligence, and negligent infliction of emotional distress. Plaintiffs seek injunctive relief, compensatory damages, statutory damages, punitive damages, reasonable attorneys' fees and costs, as well as pre- and post-judgment interest.

    The Court rejected the federal government's motion to dismiss (Google and X.AI's motion to dismiss will be considered later):.

    "The Privacy Act prohibits a federal agency from disclosing a record contained in a system of records pertaining to an individual unless the individual requests the information or consents to the disclosure in writing." To state a claim for wrongful disclosure under the Privacy Act, a plaintiff must allege facts showing that (1) the information disclosed is contained in a system of records; (2) the agency improperly disclosed the information; (3) the disclosure had an adverse effect on the plaintiff; (3) the disclosure was willful or intentional; and (4) the plaintiff suffered actual damages. The Privacy Act "provides for damages only where 'the court determines that the agency acted in a manner which was intentional or willful.'".

    For the present purpose of resolving the United States' motion to dismiss, only the third element regarding "willful or intentional" disclosure is at matter. Under the Privacy Act, willful or intentional conduct is "only somewhat greater than gross negligence," and "the Privacy Act 'imposes liability only when the agency acts in violation of the Act in a willful or intentional manner, either by committing the act without grounds for believing it to be lawful, or flagrantly disregarding others' rights under the Act.'" ….

    The United States notes that the disclosures in question were made pursuant to the Epstein Files Transparency Act ("EFTA"), which required the DOJ to release, within a 30-day period, millions of pages of documents from the DOJ's investigation of Mr. Epstein. While acknowledging that DOJ "admittedly made some mistakes, including inadvertent disclosures of victim information," the United States says that in enacting the EFTA, Congress imposed an "unprecedented" and "herculean task" upon the DOJ.

    Additionally, the United States notes that the DOJ made remedial efforts by, for example, establishing "a website through which victims could confidentially notify the [DOJ] of information that required additional redaction." In these circumstances, the United States argues that plaintiffs' allegations cannot, as a matter of law, meet the "'high hurdle'" for the requisite willful or intentional conduct….

    Plaintiffs maintain that the FAC alleges sufficient facts plausibly supporting willful or intentional conduct, including allegations that the DOJ (1) prioritized "maximum transparency" and the rapid release of information over victims' privacy interests; (2) refused victims' requests to remove the subject information, or did not respond to such requests; and (3) acted out of retaliatory motives and released files as "a punitive response to victims' public advocacy for transparency, effectively 'doxxing' victims who spoke out by exposing their identities and contact information.".

    The question of whether an agency has acted without grounds for believing the act to be lawful or has acted in flagrant disregard of others' rights under the Privacy Act depends on the context of the disclosure in each case and is a fact-intensive inquiry. Indeed, in its reply, the United States asserts that the conduct in question is measured on a continuum. If that is the case, then the United States' assertion only bolsters the conclusion that there is no "bright line" defining "willful" or "intentional" conduct, and that such matters often are not conducive to determination as a matter of law at the pleading stage….

    Viewing the facts in the light most favorable to plaintiffs, and drawing all reasonable inferences in their favor, as is required at this stage of the proceedings, the Court finds that plaintiffs have sufficiently pled facts plausibly supporting their claim that DOJ willfully or intentionally violated their rights under the Privacy Act. While the United States maintains that the mere presence of an error or mistake is not indicative of an intentional Privacy Act violation, the Court need not adopt the government's characterization of plaintiffs' allegations.

    Industry observers note that in essence, plaintiffs allege that the DOJ's disclosure of the subject materials was a "deliberate policy choice" to prioritize DOJ's obligations under the EFTA over its obligations and victims' rights under the Privacy Act. For pleading purposes, those allegations appear plausible, and are not inconsistent with the United States' assertion that DOJ was faced with a "herculean task" to accomplish within "an impossible-to-execute time frame." … [P]laintiffs' allegations that the DOJ made a deliberate decision, as a matter of policy, to give priority to its obligations under the EFTA ahead of those under the Privacy Act, are sufficient to support a plausible claim for relief….

    Recent findings suggest that elizabeth Antonia Kramer, Julie C. Erickson, and Kevin M. Osborne (Erickson Kramer Osborne LLP) represent plaintiffs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that in a last-ditch attempt to avoid Supreme Court scrutiny of its semiautomatic rifle ban, Cook County has suggested that because the last individual Petitioner in the case against it, Christopher Khaya, remarked in his deposition years ago that he wants to possess a banned Galil rifle, no Petitioner wants to possess a firearm encompassed within the question presented. (Viramontes is now known as Khaya v. Cook County.)  That argument is unpersuasive. The question presented covers "AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles," not the AR-15 alone. A Galil rifle is a semiautomatic version of the AK-47 which Cook County bans. As shown in the excerpts below, several of the amicus briefs filed in support of petitioners establish that if any rifle is "similar" to the AR-15, the Galil and other AK-types are.

    It has been revealed that "The question presented asks whether the Constitution protects possession of 'AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles.'" That framing is key because 'AR-15' does not describe a single firearm." Palmetto State Armory Br. 6.

    It has been revealed that "The list of similarly styled rifles that are commonly classified as 'assault weapons' is extensive and would include, for example: AK-47 designs, FN FALs, M1 carbines, M1As, HK 91/93/94s and CETME/PTR clones, SKSs, Kel-Tec rifles, Thompsons, Ruger Mini-14/Mini-30s, FN SCARs, and Steyr AUGs and other bullpup designs. These rifles are likewise banned under most 'assault weapons' laws, including the laws at matter here. It is therefore essential to measure their popularity as well—not just that of the AR-15, which is but one instance of the banned firearm type." English Br. 13.

    "Thus, in Smith & Wesson Brands, Inc. v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos, 605 U.S. 280 (2025), this Court unanimously explained that so-called 'military style' assault weapons, … includ[ing] AR-15 rifles, AK-47 rifles, and .50 caliber sniper rifles,' are 'both widely legal and bought by many ordinary consumers,' and '[t]he AR-15 is the most popular rifle in the country.' Id. at 297." GOA Br. 19.

    Sources indicate that "A Memphis man used a semiautomatic rifle to shoot two armed robbers who were 'ransack[ing]' his house. Action News 5, Homeowner shoots, kills 2 burglars with AK-47 (June 1, 2018), https://perma.cc/J47A-PFUV." Tennessee Br. 14.

    Sources indicate that "AR-15s and similar rifles have different characteristics that appeal to different consumers, but all are semiautomatic rifles at heart." Eleven State-Based Firearms Advocacy Organizations Br. 16.

    "Semiautomatic operation fires one round for each trigger activation and uses the energy of firing to chamber the next round. That basic mechanism has been commercially available for generations." Rocky Mountain Gun Owners Br. 9.

    My comment: Obviously, whether it is an AK-47 or AR-15, a semiautomatic action uses gas from firing a round to do the "autoloading function," so if semiautomatic rifles are to be protected under the Second Amendment, it should not matter whether the Court rules in a case involving an AR-15 semiautomatic rifle or an AK-47 style semiautomatic rifle.

    • "But the M16 is capable of burst or fully automatic fire, meaning that a shooter can fire multiple rounds with a single function of the trigger.
    • "Semiautomatic rifles are in common use among law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At issue in Viramontes (now Khaya) v. Cook County in the Supreme Court is the difference between fully automatic firearms such as the M-16 and semiautomatic rifles including the AR-15 platform. The following are a few excerpts from four amicus briefs establishing that the difference is fundamental.

    "But the M16 is capable of burst or fully automatic fire, meaning that a shooter can fire multiple rounds with a single function of the trigger. See Staples, 511 U.S. at 603. Fully automatic firearms 'were never in widespread civilian use' and have 'traditionally been banned' in the United States. Heller II, 670 F.3d at 1287 (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting). The AR-15, by contrast, is a semiautomatic firearm, meaning that it fires only one shot with each function of the trigger. See Cargill, 602 U.S. at 410–411, 416."  U.S. Br. 28.

    "Semiautomatic rifles are in common use among law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes. 'The first commercially available semi-automatic rifles * * * entered the market between 1903 and 1906.' Heller II, 670 F.3d at 1287 (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting). Semiautomatic rifles 'have not traditionally been banned,' or even subjected to heavy regulation. Id. at 1269. Instead, they 'traditionally have been widely accepted as lawful possessions.' Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600, 612 (1994)." U.S. Br. 19–20.

    Industry observers note that "A semiautomatic firearm fires one bullet for each trigger pull, while an automatic weapon (machine gun) fires continuously until the ammunition supply is exhausted, so long as the shooter presses and holds the trigger. See Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600, 602 n.1 (1994). 'The AR-15 is the civilian version of the military's M-16 rifle, and is…a semiautomatic weapon. The M-16, in contrast, is a selective fire rifle that allows the operator…to choose semiautomatic or automatic fire.' Id. at 603." Ballistic Experts Br. 6.

    "Nor is an AR-15 'almost the same gun' as the military's M16 in the critical respect identified by federal law. Bevis, 85 F.4th at 1195. An ordinary AR-15 is semiautomatic: each trigger pull fires one round. A machinegun, by contrast, 'shoots, is designed to shoot, or can be readily restored to shoot, automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger.' 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b). That operational difference—not appearance or lineage—separates an ordinary semiautomatic AR-15 from an automatic machinegun." Cruz Br. 21.

    Recent findings suggest that "In 1963, Colt submitted to the predecessor agency of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) two firearms for evaluation: a semiautomatic 'AR-15 Sports Version Rifle' and an 'AR-15 automatic rifle' (later renamed the M16). The agency found that modifications to the automatic version that made it into the Sports Version 'have changed the weapon in basic design to the extent that it is not a "firearm" in the machine gun category' as defined in the National Firearms Act." Second Amendment Law Center Br. 3.

    According to recent reports, the amicus briefs in Khaya v. Cook County that best explain the critical distinction between a fully automatic machine gun like an M16 and a semiautomatic AR-15 are these:.

    Brief of Ballistic Experts and Second Amendment Law Professors at 6–8.

    Brief of Second Amendment Law Center at 3–6.

    Wall Street delivered its verdict on the blue-wave midterms 48 hours later in the form of a red wave—red ink, that is.

    After a brief relief rally the day after the election, the Dow shed more than 1,800 points, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5% and into correction territory, and roughly $2.5 trillion in market value vanished in a single session. Nvidia alone dropped more than 8%.

    It has been revealed that market participants watched the collapse of the AI trade in real time—the bet that a massive buildout of data centers, chips, and software would power faster growth, higher productivity and rising wages for years to come. That theory hit the brick wall of an incoming Congress that has AI and data centers on their blacklist.

    Democrats, who will comfortably control the Senate and hold their largest House majority in nearly two decades, have been far more hostile to data centers and AI than Republicans have. Several of their biggest wins came in places such as Texas, where local opposition to new data centers had been building.

    Investors can read the writing on the wall: more regulation and taxation, slower permitting, and lower profits for AI and AI-adjacent companies. Since equity prices are ultimately justified by future earnings, adjusting those future expectations down also drove down equity prices.

    >>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI.

    The fallout goes well beyond Silicon Valley. AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.

    Recent findings suggest that the fiscal picture is dimmer, too. With Democrats running both chambers, there is no chance of further tax reform or meaningful spending cuts for at least two years. If a Republican Congress couldn't bring itself to enshrine the DOGE savings into law, a Democratic one certainly won't.

    Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer fresh commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

    Aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

    Those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

    >>> Slowing Data Center Construction Signals the Need for Pro-Growth Reforms.

    Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

    So the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.

    The administration retains broad authority to issue executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

    Recent findings suggest that democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.

    In a recent development, the president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or upcoming regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.

    According to recent reports, the economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

    #136967. The U.S. Navy Needs a Upcoming Battlecruiser. Will It Get One?

    The U.S. Navy Needs a Upcoming Battlecruiser. Will It Get One?

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding proposal called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a latest, modern class of battleship.
    • Sources indicate that last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding blueprint called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a newly introduced, modern class of battleship.
    • Industry observers note that by any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding proposal called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a latest, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.The U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” WarshipThe unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.>>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”The Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.The damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile launches, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.>>> To Build the Golden FleetHow the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol HillWhile battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.Keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.Resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious plan, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

    Sources indicate that last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding blueprint called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a newly introduced, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.

    Industry observers note that by any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.

    Sources indicate that the U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” Warship.

    The unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.

    Recent findings suggest that >>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”.

    In a recent development, the Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.

    In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.

    The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.

    According to recent reports, the damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile releases, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.

    >>> To Build the Golden Fleet.

    How the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol Hill.

    While battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing new or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.

    Industry observers note that keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.

    In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.

    According to recent reports, resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious plan, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.

    This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

    Latest Update: Fifth Circuit Dismisses Lawsuit Over Facebook Removal, Supposedly Connected to Stanford Internet Observatory, of COVID-Related Post

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, from Hines v.
    • Sources indicate that jill Hines sued Stanford University, Alex Stamos, and others, alleging they conspired with the government to censor her online speech about COVID-19.
    • Recent findings suggest that this case is closely related to Murthy v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, from Hines v. Stamos, decided yesterday by Judges W. Eugene Davis, Leslie Southwick, and Stuart Kyle Duncan:.

    Sources indicate that jill Hines sued Stanford University, Alex Stamos, and others, alleging they conspired with the government to censor her online speech about COVID-19. The district court dismissed her suit without prejudice for lack of subject-matter and personal jurisdiction. Because Hines has not shown that her injury is fairly traceable to Stanford or Stamos, she lacks standing. We therefore AFFIRM without reaching personal jurisdiction….

    Recent findings suggest that this case is closely related to Murthy v. Missouri, which guides our resolution of this appeal. In Murthy, Hines (along with others) sued federal officials and agencies, alleging the government censored her online speech against COVID-19 restrictions in violation of the First Amendment. Here, Hines challenges Defendants' participation in an academic project named the Election Integrity Partnership (EIP). She alleges the EIP and its participants aided the government's scheme to have Facebook suppress her online speech, also in violation of the First Amendment. {Our review is limited to Hines's claims against Stanford and Alex Stamos, the former director of the Stanford Internet Observatory, which was an EIP member.}.

    It has been revealed that facebook began moderating COVID-19 content early in the pandemic, deleting or demoting posts it deemed false. In April 2020 alone, it labeled roughly 50 million pieces of content. That same month, Hines launched a grassroots campaign to challenge COVID-19 government restrictions and used Facebook to communicate with her supporters. She was aware of Facebook's moderation and took deliberate measures to circumvent it.

    The EIP, a consortium of researchers and institutions, was formed in July 2020. It sought to identify misinformation about elections and voting. For about three months in 2020, it monitored elections-related content on social media. EIP participants sometimes recommended actions to social-media platforms and logged their communications when they did. In most instances, the platforms took no detectable action on those recommendations….

    To have standing, a "plaintiff must have (1) suffered an injury in fact, (2) that is fairly traceable to the challenged conduct of the defendant, and (3) that is likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision." For the claims before us, the second inquiry—traceability of Hines's past injuries—is "the whole ball game." ….

    Sources indicate that there is one injury that Hines claims is traceable to Defendants: on September 9, 2020, Facebook removed a post from Hines's page that attached an article entitled Masks Don't Work. At the time, Facebook explained the post went "against our Community Standards." It also reduced distribution of Hines's page on COVID-19 restrictions for "repeated" violations of its standards on "Inauthentic Behavior" and for "repeated sharing of false news." Hines does not dispute that these restrictions fit Facebook's own content moderation….

    Hines's traceability theory rests on an inference drawn from timing. On September 8, 2020, the EIP received a massive submission of over 200 webpages and social-media posts from the Democratic National Committee. Among those 200 webpages was a single post by Hines where she encouraged her followers to lobby their representatives to end the COVID-19 public-health emergency. In Hines's view, the one-day timing between the DNC's submission and Facebook's moderation of her page is evidence that EIP participants called Facebook's attention to her single post in the 200-webpage DNC submission.

    We are not persuaded by her argument. Discovery revealed no communication between the EIP and Facebook about Hines, and Facebook did not remove or moderate the post that the EIP received. {Hines argues there may be evidence of Defendants' communications with Facebook in undiscovered Slack or Zoom messages. But Stanford produced "communications and other documents" mentioning Hines or her account, and Hines neither challenged that production nor moved to compel additional discovery, although the scheduling order allowed for that. The mere possibility of undiscovered communications that were not sought in the district court is not evidence.}.

    According to recent reports, A notation in the EIP's records even states Hines's COVID-19 posts were beyond the scope of the EIP's elections-oriented work. We conclude as a matter of law that timing alone is too attenuated to trace Hines's injury to Defendants.

    Murthy also requires us to consider Facebook's own incentives to moderate content. Facebook gave its own reasons for acting when it removed Hines's post and demoted her page, and Hines does not dispute that that moderation aligned with Facebook's COVID-19 policies. We agree with the district court that there's no indication that Facebook, in moderating Hines's post, did anything other than follow its own moderation policy….

    I am not at all involved with Stanford's defense of this lawsuit.

    Elisabeth S. Theodore, John B. Bellinger, III, R. Stanton Jones, and Stephen K. Wirth (Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer, L.L.P.) and James A. Brown (Liskow & Lewis, A.P.L.C.) represent defendants.
