But politicians can’t address all these factors of the affordability crisis, without understanding one of its largest contributors.

    Sources indicate that the Iran war obviously caused serious disruptions to global energy markets, and the resultant shortfall in supply drove up prices. Even with some oil and natural gas moving through the Strait of Hormuz, the cost to move that product is up dramatically as expenses like insurance have exploded.

    Since energy affects the price of everything we do and buy, more expensive energy pushes up prices throughout the economy. This occurs not only because of things like higher transportation costs, but also because energy is used to make many products too.

    Virtually all plastic in our lives is synthesized from either oil or natural gas. This includes countless products from automotive parts to polyester clothing, but also cosmetics to pharmaceuticals. Almost all fertilizer is also made from oil and gas.

    >>> Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy Shock.

    Since energy is an input for so many products sold to consumers and industry alike, the effects of price changes are far-reaching, though it takes time for consumers to feel the full effect.

    Industry observers note that for example, consumers are only recently experiencing the higher food prices stemming from energy market disruptions that started eight months ago. As farmers paid more for diesel and fertilizer, they began passing those costs on through supply chains via distributors, wholesalers, and grocers.

    But the cost of the war goes beyond consumer prices, as evidenced by the monthly Treasury statement for October. Spending on national defense last month spiked, hitting $129 billion—up 44.9 percent from September. That was a key contributor to the worst deficit ever for October: $404 billion. And military spending for this fiscal year is projected to exceed $1.1 trillion.

    According to recent reports, all that additional spending and borrowing is adding to the national debt and costing taxpayers, both today and in the future. The cost to service the $41 trillion debt has become genuinely massive. Gross interest on the debt equaled 32.3 percent of all tax receipts in October, a figure projected to worsen.

    Excessive government spending and borrowing is further fueling inflation, a tax on today’s savers and wage earners that has also robbed more than 30 percent of the dollar’s value since the start of 2020.

    But the flood of debt issuance has also greatly increased the demand for loanable funds, or savings. That increased demand puts upward pressure on the price for loanable funds, which is the interest rate. The government is borrowing so much money that its crowding out the private sector and increasing interest rates on everything from mortgages to auto loans.

    >>> Overseas Wars Put Affordability on Hold, but That’s Only Temporary.

    According to recent reports, that’s a key reason why homeownership affordability, which had improved to a three-year high in February, has fallen each month since the Iran war started as interest rates marched relentlessly higher. Those higher interest rates also stem from inflation expectations rising due to the war’s energy market disruptions.

    In a recent development, that’s created a deadly combination for the housing market where both home prices and interest rates have risen dramatically in recent years. That one-two punch has made housing unaffordable and cratered home sales.

    It now takes more than half of the median household’s after-tax income to afford the monthly mortgage payment on a median price home. For families whose budgets are already strapped from high consumer prices, homeownership is simply out of reach.

    According to recent reports, unfortunately, there’s more pain to come from what’s already working its way through supply chains. Those price increases will eventually work their way to consumer prices too.

    #136943. A Study In Red, White and Blue: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle in the USA

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1418 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    A Study In Red, White and Blue: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle in the USA

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When I was choosing the setting for my new book, The Mark of Moriarty, which re-imagines the titular Professor survived his last battle with Sherlock Holmes, I found myself genuinely spoiled for choice.
    • Holmes, for all his fantastical adventures, rarely travelled beyond London, glimpsing the wider world only when it came to his doorstep.
    • He can go anywhere in the world except his homeland.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When I was choosing the setting for my new book, The Mark of Moriarty, which re-imagines the titular Professor survived his last battle with Sherlock Holmes, I found myself genuinely spoiled for choice.

    Holmes, for all his fantastical adventures, rarely travelled beyond London, glimpsing the wider world only when it came to his doorstep. Professor Moriarty, presumed dead post-Reichenbach and presumably still notorious in the UK, is in the exact opposite position.

    He can go anywhere in the world except his homeland.

    In a recent development, while I was scouring the globe for an interesting place to send the master criminal, I kept coming back to a recurring theme in Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s books. Indeed, even as a child, reading the classic Holmes adventures, one thought kept jumping out at me….

    “Wow, this guy really likes the USA.”.

    In a recent development, as I grew up, I discovered just how true this is. Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s enthusiasm with the United States was a matter of public record. He took great inspiration from this newfound nation, recovering from a civil war and forging its future before his eyes.

    In the process of looking into this transatlantic fascination, I thought I’d share some weird and wonderful findings about Doyle’s brushes with the states, his encounters with citizens of that nation…  and one confrontation with a visitor from Atlantis.

    Sources indicate that even before he set foot in the States, Doyle devoured news from America. In fact, factions and societies from the USA featured prominently throughout his work and across the Sherlock Holmes canon.

    According to recent reports, when he was just twenty-one years old, Doyle anonymously published “An American’s Tale”, a short story in which an Englishman is accused of murdering a rival in Arizona. Taking the Englishman to “Flytrap Gulch” to hang him for his crime, the supposed victim is unexpectedly discovered inside… a giant man-eating plant.

    One of Doyle’s more fantastical tales, it certainly paints the USA as a strange and undiscovered country.

    As he embarked on the Holmes canon, Doyle still injected America into his stories, with a particular interest in the factions and societies across the pond.

    His story, “The Five Orange Pips” features allusions to the infamous KKK. His final of the Sherlock Holmes novels, The Valley of Fear, was born out of his fascination with the Molly Maguires, a secret society that engaged in radical industrial action against Pennsylvanian mining companies, and the Pinkertons, the brutal detective agency who were hired to stop them.

    Doyle’s enthusiasm for American goings-on did sometimes outpace his knowledge, however, particularly due to his reliance on secondary sources which filtered to the UK.

    Holmes’ very first appearance, A Study In Scarlet, featured an organisation called the Danites, an avenging division of the Mormon Church’s mysterious “Council of Four”.

    While the Danites certainly existed, historians consider them a short-lived faction based in mid-century Missouri, and far from the organised assassin squad from the book, with Doyle’s own daughter explaining that her father “would be the first to admit that his first Sherlock Holmes novel was full of errors about the Mormons”.

    For the record, there’s no evidence that he believed in man-eating plants.

    Eventually, shortly after Sherlock met his end at the Reichenbach Falls, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle finally visited America for the first time.

    It has been revealed that the Sherlock Holmes stories had proceeded him. He was met with an incredible reception from his already prominent U.S. fanbase, with the Boston Globe reporting him as; well proportioned, attractive and with a handsome face.

    In his journeys, Arthur Conan Doyle only grew fonder of America; reporting an incredible time spent on an elevator in Manhattan’s Woolworth Building, whose speed he compared to an artillery weapon, and defending the USA against nitpicking critics by saying;.

    “Every globe-trotter has paragraphs about the number of spittoons in a hotel bar (as if it matters!)”.

    Doyle also fell in love with the sport of baseball, to the point of committing a cardinal sin for any Brit; suggesting British football teams should adopt the sport.

    “I will venture to say, that if this was done, we should in a few years have as many to see a baseball final between Tottenham Hotspur and Preston North End as come now to the football.

    As to the furore which a decent British team, could we evolve one, would create in America, it is impossible to exaggerate it.”.

    Sadly, the United Kingdom has failed to assemble Doyle’s dream team.

    Despite the international success of his books, it was his forays into Spiritualism which brought Doyle back to the United States in the 1920’s, and which brought him in contact with his most prominent trans-atlantic friendship.

    One of the dramas that marked Doyle’s later American travels was his fractious friendship with magician Harry Houdini.

    Admirers of each other’s work, Doyle and Houdini held the opposite opinions on the supernatural that one might expect. Doyle, the creator of super-logician Sherlock Holmes, had become a devout spiritualist, while the magician Houdini was an ardent sceptic.

    Strangely enough, so strong was Doyle’s belief, that he insisted Houdini’s escapist tricks involved some form of magic, refusing to budge when Houdini himself told him otherwise.

    In a recent development, “My dear chap.” Doyle wrote in a letter to his friend. “Why do you go around the world seeking a demonstration of the occult when you are giving one all the time?”.

    Houdini even invited Doyle to the annual dinner at the Society of American Magicians. As a prank, and to prove Magicians could be fooled as much as they claimed Spiritualists were, Doyle screened footage of “live dinosaurs” to an astounded audience.

    These live dinosaurs would prove to be stop-motion animations, taken from the upcoming film adaptation of Doyle’s novel; The Lost World.

    Despite their spirited back and forth, tensions between the pair came to a head during a 1922 visit to Atlantic City, where Doyle’s wife Jean, channelled Houdini’s mother at a séance. The incident forced Houdini to publicly denounce the events in question, placing Doyle & Houdini publicly at odds.

    It was on his Spiritualism tour that Doyle had the strangest encounter Doyle he would perhaps have in America, when Doyle met one of his fans, an old Colonel from the South.

    While in Cleveland, described unflatteringly by Doyle as “a grim city of iron and shipping”, Doyle was advancing his lectures on Spiritualism, when he was confronted by an old Southern Colonel with an incredible story to tell.

    “The Colonel thought he was an Atlantean by origin,” Doyle reported, with the Colonel continuing to explain that his mother was the former Atlantean Queen.

    Though the author tolerated this eccentric visitor in the daytime, when the Colonel revealed up at his hotel room at night, with a message from the former Queen, Doyle was forced to confront the more troubling side of fandom.

    In the end, long after Doyle’s love-affair with the USA began, Sherlock Holmes himself finally set foot in the States.

    It was in 1917, in “The Final Bow”, the last story in the Sherlock Holmes canon, that the detective confirmed he had crossed the Atlantic, travelling to Chicago and beyond.

    It’s a fitting end to a canon which, despite taking place primarily in London, is so deeply suffused with Doyle’s love for the States.

    The more I’ve learned about it, the more of a privilege it has seemed, to get the chance to send the iconic Professor to 1890’s Newly introduced York.

    A place full of the societies, mysticism and people his creator adored so much, where he’ll pull in to the same dock that Sir Arthur Conan Doyle did when he first set foot in America.

    Jack Anderson is a UK-based writer of horror and mystery fiction. Jack got his start writing for the internet, penning the viral serial "Has Anyone Heard of the Left/Right Game?," which he wrote in a caffeine-fueled haze. It has since been adapted into a hit QCODE podcast starring Tessa Thompson in the leading role of Alice. His debut thriller, The Grief Doctor, was published by Raven Books in June 2024. Jack is also developing a number of original television and film ideas across the horror genre. He lives with his wife in Sheffield. Lifelong fans of games and puzzles, together they’re burning through every escape room in the North of England.

    Court Blocks FCC from Early Review of ABC Broadcast Licenses

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From today's decision by Judge Loren Alikhan (D.D.C.) in ABC, Inc.
    • Plaintiffs assert that Defendants violated their First Amendment rights by designating their broadcast licenses for early renewal as retaliation for Plaintiffs' broadcasting unfavorable speech about President Donald J.
    • Recent findings suggest that because broadcast media requires access to radio spectrum to operate, and because radio spectrum is a finite public resource, the FCC is responsible for granting and renewing broadcast licenses….
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From today's decision by Judge Loren Alikhan (D.D.C.) in ABC, Inc. v. FCC:.

    Plaintiffs assert that Defendants violated their First Amendment rights by designating their broadcast licenses for early renewal as retaliation for Plaintiffs' broadcasting unfavorable speech about President Donald J. Trump and the Republican Party….

    Recent findings suggest that because broadcast media requires access to radio spectrum to operate, and because radio spectrum is a finite public resource, the FCC is responsible for granting and renewing broadcast licenses…. The FCC may grant an initial license or a license renewal for a term of no more than eight years, and it "ordinarily" grants licenses for eight-year terms, with term dates staggered by the geographic location of each station. "However, if the FCC finds that the public interest, convenience and necessity will be served thereby, it may glitch either an initial license or a renewal thereof for a lesser term." ….

    It has been revealed that the FCC argued that the ABC licenses were being designated for early review because the FCC was investigating the possibility that Disney and ABC were discriminating in employment for "DEI" reasons. But Judge Alikhan concluded that this was likely a pretext, and the likely real reason for the FCC's action was unconstitutional Administration retaliation against ABC's speech:.

    "Courts have recognized that [] circumstantial evidence, including proximity in time between the protected speech and government's adverse actions, the defendant's expression of hostility to the protected speech, and the absence of a proffered legitimate alternative explanation for the action[,] can support a finding that protected speech caused the agency's response.".

    Here, robust circumstantial evidence strongly supports Plaintiffs' theory of causation. Although Defendants proffer a legitimate alternative explanation, the court does not find that explanation to be credible on the record before the court. Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now. What started in 2020 as questions about how ABC "can keep getting a license" if it "report[s] fake news" has crescendoed into repeated calls for the Commission to strip ABC's broadcast licenses for their editorial decisions.

    The court counts eleven such calls made by President Trump over the past two years—the most recent being in July 2026. See ECF No. 1 ("When you have a network and you have evening shows, and all they do is hit Trump[,] … I think maybe their license should be taken away. It will be up to [Chairman] Carr."); ECF No. 2-3, at 109-10 ("[T]hey ought to take away [ABC's] license."); id. at 157 ("ABC's license should be TERMINATED."); id. at 166 ("CBS should lose its license, and it should be bid out to the Highest Bidder, as should all other Broadcast Licenses, because they are just as corrupt as CBS—and maybe even WORSE!"); id. at 252 ("I think ABC should lose its license."); id. at 303 ("ABC & NBC FAKE NEWS … SHOULD, ACCORDING TO MANY, HAVE THEIR LICENSES REVOKED BY THE FCC."); id. at 306 ("ABC and NBC FAKE NEWS … should lose their Licenses."); id. at 321 ("[T]he Federal Communications Commission should look into the license of … ABC Fake News."); id. at 340 ("I think the license should be taken away from ABC because your news is so fake and it's so wrong. And we have a great commissioner, the chairman, who should look at that."); ECF No. 2-4, at 13 ("If Network NEWSCASTS, and their Late Night Shows, are almost 100% Negative to President Donald J. Trump, MAGA, and the Republican Party, shouldn't their very valuable Broadcast Licenses be terminated? I say, YES!"); id. at 99 ("ABC fake news ha[s] [] remarked that [it] would not cover this speech…. Fraud like this should mean a revocation of their licenses.").

    To be sure, President Trump is within his rights "to persuade Americans, including by speaking forcefully or critically, in ways that [he] believes would advance the public interest." Here, however, the President's persistent "rhetoric demonstrates that [he] harbored animosity" toward Plaintiffs because of their protected speech, specifically—to quote the President—their "negative" and "unfair coverage" of him and the Republican Party.

    Sources indicate that what is more, Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders. The same week he was tapped to be President Trump's FCC chair, following months of President Trump's calling for "ABC [to] lose its license" for how it covered the presidential campaign, then-Commissioner Carr lauded "license revocation" as a "remedy" to "deter this kind of conduct." Then, early in his tenure as chairman and after committing himself to President Trump's agenda, Chairman Carr ordered the Enforcement Bureau to investigate Disney's employment practices, and soon ordered another investigation into The View.

    According to recent reports, when President Trump first called for Mr. Kimmel to be fired—as well as for ABC's license to be "taken away"—Chairman Carr vowed to intervene if Plaintiffs did not "take action on Kimmel." Months later, when President Trump decried Mr. Kimmel's skit about the First Lady, the Commission, at Chairman Carr's behest, initiated early license renewal proceedings the next day. Chairman Carr said of the move, "If you didn't take us seriously, now you should.".

    Most recently, when President Trump touted that Plaintiffs' not broadcasting his address justifies "revocation of their licenses," Chairman Carr unveiled that the Commission was "looking into" Plaintiffs' decision, and that he expected it to come up during the early license renewal proceedings. This conduct and rhetoric are "powerful evidence of [Defendants'] retaliatory motive.".

    Sources indicate that in response, Defendants point to Chairman Carr's assurances that the Commission "has not singled out any one organization for special treatment," and will remain "open-minded" throughout the early license renewal proceedings. But these assurances fall flat when Chairman Carr is simultaneously making comments that the Commission is "looking into" Plaintiffs' "decision [not] to air" a presidential address as part of the proceedings, especially given that Chairman Carr has noted that this specific presidential address is "something that broadcasters should be carrying.".

    Turning to temporal proximity, against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr's call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel's skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings. Indeed, in the wake of Mr. Kimmel's September 2025 comments about President Trump and his supporters, Chairman Carr stated, "We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.".

    It has been revealed that chairman Carr made this promise at the same time that President Trump said of the situation: "When you have a network and you have evening demonstrates, and all they do is hit Trump[,] … I think maybe their license should be taken away. It will be up to [Chairman] Carr." Chairman Carr's "fast-moving" inquest into Plaintiffs' business operations and editorial decisions from the moment he was appointed as chairman and seemingly at the President's direction further "indicates [Defendants'] retaliatory animus." ….

    The court therefore enjoined the FCC from "from taking any continuing or further action against Plaintiffs in relation to the early license renewal proceedings before the Federal Communications Commission, including issuing a Hearing Designation Order;".

    Becoming a teacher is no way to get rich, but becoming the head of a teachers union? That’s a different story.

    Take Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, who received $546,158 in total compensation last year, according to the union’s latest financial disclosure.

    That’s over seven times the $74,495 average salary earned by public-school teachers nationwide.

    And the new documents, recently filed with the federal Labor Department, show that an AFT president’s cronies can profit handsomely, too.

    Outside consultants, a Fresh York law firm, a public-relations firm and others appear to have raked in more than $2.2 million from AFT coffers to help Weingarten produce her 2025 book “Why Fascists Fear Teachers”—up from the more than $1.4 million previously estimated by the Freedom Foundation and reported by The Post.

    The payments break down across two filings, covering two separate fiscal years.

    >>> Randi Weingarten’s Dirty Back-to-School War on Target.

    The first, for a one-year period from 2024 to 2025, documented substantial costs connected to the book paid by the AFT—including payments to Weingarten’s literary agent Inkwell Management, to a fact-checker credited in her acknowledgments, and to a photographer for her author’s headshot.

    The upcoming form adds further amounts apparently related to the same project.

    According to recent reports, on Sept. 25, 2025, nine days after the book’s release, the AFT paid Inkwell Management $28,125 for a “publication expense,” bringing combined payments to the agent across both filings to $92,215.

    Separately, the union paid Feldman Strategies, a publicity firm, $202,500; shortly after the pub date, the PR group posted, “It has been a true honor for our entire team at Feldman Strategies to help promote” Weingarten’s book.

    According to recent reports, the latest filing also records an $80,000 “royalty payment” sent on Oct. 23, 2025, to a limited liability firm controlled by Weingarten.

    That sum follows a $125,000 royalty payment to the same entity disclosed in the union’s prior annual report, bringing the combined royalty transfers from AFT to the Weingarten-controlled company to $205,000.

    And in its 2026 filing, the union paid Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler LLP — the law firm credited in the book with reviewing Weingarten’s manuscript—another $591,174, bringing cumulative legal fees to the firm across both years to nearly $1.6 million.

    The union says the firm toiled on the book “pro bono,” but the attorneys’ extensive financial ties to the AFT create an obvious incentive to characterize that work as such.

    The royalty payments require additional explanation: Public filings show the AFT itself receiving publisher advances connected to the book, then disbursing a portion of those funds as a “royalty payment” to Teachers Want What Kids Need, LLC—an entity controlled by Weingarten.

    The publisher did not pay royalties to Weingarten or her LLC directly; the money flowed through the union, in an arrangement that remains opaque.

    Weingarten has stated that some of the book’s proceeds would go back to the AFT, the AFT Disaster Relief Fund, and the AFT Educational Foundation.

    Even if that claim holds, dues-paying teachers shouldn’t be required to subsidize a book project that profits their union’s president.

    In July, the GOP-led House Committee on Education and the Workforce opened a formal inquiry into the matter based on The Post’s initial report, requesting documents on the AFT’s book-related expenditures, contracts and royalty flows.

    That inquiry is controlled by the committee majority, however—and once Democrats take control of the House in January, the probe is expected to stall or be closed.

    The minority can still request materials and concern reports, but it cannot compel the same level of investigation.

    Separately, the Department of Labor’s Inspector General has already opened its own review to probe whether union dues were improperly used for Weingarten’s book project.

    That executive-branch inquiry can continue under President Donald Trump’s administration, regardless of which party controls Congress.

    >>> Randi Weingarten’s Convention Exposes the Teachers’ Union as a Political Machine.

    The new 2026 filing supplies further evidence that any ongoing review should examine: The additional royalty payment, the fresh publication expense routed to the literary agent, the large PR contract and the further $591,174 to Patterson Belknap all post-date the period covered by the prior report.

    Payments to the Weingarten-controlled entity, the literary agent, the PR firm and the consultants raise questions about whether dues money collected from teachers was used for the personal benefit of the union’s top officer.

    Federal labor filings exist precisely so that members and the public can review such expenditures.

    When these records show repeated transfers linked to an officer’s private project, the disclosures themselves supply the basis for scrutiny.

    Teachers who don’t want their hard-earned paychecks to underwrite an officer’s vanity project have a practical alternative.

    Organizations such as the Teacher Freedom Alliance offer membership—including free liability insurance—without routing teacher dues to electoral campaigns or left-wing causes.

    If enough fed-up teachers leave the AFT, people like Randi Weingarten might think twice about wasting members’ money on personal and political pet projects.

    #136936. Quinn Connor on body horror, queerness, academia, and southern gothic novels

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3696 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Quinn Connor on body horror, queerness, academia, and southern gothic novels

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that your Beloved Remains is the third novel by Quinn Connor, and sits alongside their other Southern gothic stories.
    • According to recent reports, after discovering the school might be closing, Celia finds a lost manuscript by the school’s founder, a feminist writer and heiress whose life and work has cast a long shadow over the school and its reputation.
    • The book is part mystery, part gothic horror, part dark academia, part dysfunctional romance, though that doesn’t do justice to the strangeness of the book, the atmosphere, the ideas around literature and the university that are thrown around—and just how much fun it all is.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that your Beloved Remains is the third novel by Quinn Connor, and sits alongside their other Southern gothic stories. This novel is set at Basin College, a small school in a remote part of Arkansas where Celia Kiel, the school’s archivist, has spent her whole life.

    According to recent reports, after discovering the school might be closing, Celia finds a lost manuscript by the school’s founder, a feminist writer and heiress whose life and work has cast a long shadow over the school and its reputation. Working from a partial manuscript she found pickled in formaldehyde, she teams up with Joan Harriot, a literature postdoc, who is not just a gifted mimic but Celia’s academic nemesis, to forge and reconstruct the book in an effort to save the school.

    The book is part mystery, part gothic horror, part dark academia, part dysfunctional romance, though that doesn’t do justice to the strangeness of the book, the atmosphere, the ideas around literature and the university that are thrown around—and just how much fun it all is.

    The book tells the story of a very dysfunctional pair writing a manuscript, and so we reached out to Dr. Robyn Barrow and Alex Cronin, the writing duo behind Quinn Connor to ask about how they write together without trying to kill each other, academia, queer Southern stories, body horror, and how their writing surprises the people who know them.

    AD: I really enjoyed Your Beloved Remains, which was so much fun. Maybe fun is the wrong word?

    AD: From the beginning of your writing career, I’m sure people have asked, how do the two of you work together? Here you have written a book that is explicitly about a literary partnership. Was this kind of inevitable?

    AC: It probably was a little bit inevitable, because it’s always been interesting to us. Just rapidly on the way we work: We’ve been doing this for thirteen years now. The way it works is that I have a character, Robyn has a character, and then we bring them in conversation. We are often literally passing the laptop back and forth, line by line, switching who writes it. So it ends up being super seamless.

    Of course, over thirteen years, I think we have learned enough about it to know how bad it could be if we did not truly like each other. We have strong boundaries with co-writing. We get along. We have a lot of the same tastes. We love each other. These are the things that make co-writing safe.

    In a recent development, but because it’s so safe for us, it was really fun to explore [the question], “but what if it wasn’t safe?” Because it is so vulnerable to be co-writing and sharing a creative project. To share that can feel really scary. So what if the worst thing happened? What if all of those hurt feelings that could exist grew into something wild and terrifying?

    Industry observers note that AD: There is a scene where, not to spoil too much, but Celia gets those first pages back and she goes, this is horrible. Because she can’t give or take criticism well. But she’s also in pain because it’s so good and she knows she could never have written it, so she’s overwhelmed by anger and jealousy.

    AC: Robyn and I are very lucky because we have similar standards and we have similar but different talents. We’re very compatible, but co-writing with someone who is not compatible would be really difficult. Celia finds herself in this position where she just is struggling to keep up and that is a horror for her because she wants to be the keeper of Beatrice. The keeper of this archive and of her voice. And she can’t do it. The way that Harriot describes it is Celia is “a high priestess who can’t hear the voice of god.”.

    According to recent reports, AD: Which is such a great phrase, but the book resembles a lot of different genres. It’s gothic, it’s dark academia. Robyn, I know you work in academia, so I’m sure you have thoughts on the genre.

    RB: We have always loved Donna Tartt and The Secret History. We loved it and around 2017, 2018, it felt like suddenly the internet discovered it. It was everywhere and it sort of ballooned into this whole genre, “dark academia.”.

    It’s great that there are so many people enjoying reading and writing this genre, but it has gone quite far from The Secret History. Now there’s dark academic fantasy and all these versions that, to me, have nothing to do with academia. They’re not really exploring the themes of the university that I find interesting.

    It has been revealed that when I pitched the idea for Your Beloved Remains to Alex, I was like, “We’re gonna make this call from inside the house.” This is about academic frustration. The kind of rage that can build up in an eternal grad program.

    Recent findings suggest that when I came up with the pitch, I was in the sixth year of an eight-year grad program. A lot of Harriot’s struggles with her career and the feelings that she has about being a postdoc, was cathartic for me to write through. Hopefully it gets back to some of the roots of dark academia. We’re re-coining this book as “academic horror.”.

    AC: I’m just going to parrot what I’ve heard Robyn say before, which is that often these books focus on the students, but in our book, the students are not really a part of it. It’s about the institution. The students can leave on holiday break. They get to go home. This is about the people that don’t leave. Where the university is their life. Which, for Robyn, has been a really good thing.

    It has been revealed that RB: It’s funny because since I wrote the book, I have gone on to finish my PhD and get a tenure-track job, which is like winning the lottery. That was never in the cards for Harriot. Harriot was never destined for tenure. [laughs].

    According to recent reports, AC: It’s kind of the same thing as the collaboration question. It’s an exploration of the dark side and the horrible “what if things had gone a different way.”.

    Industry observers note that AD: There’s an exchange in the book. “What does it mean to want something so much you end up destroying it?” Harriot answers “it sounds like doing a PhD in the humanities.”.

    According to recent reports, RB: [laughs] Exactly! Sometimes you make the thing that you love your job, which I would say is true both in academia and as an author. You make writing that you love the thing that you make money off of, and then you spend so long grinding that you actually ruin it. Harriot is so burnt out. She clearly came to being a literary scholar because she loved reading, and now she’s so cynical and so lost because of all the years of struggle with that.

    AD: You noted that students are kind of the point of academia, but they’re only there for a few years, but there are people who spend their whole lives there.

    In a recent development, RB: Since most people who write books about academia have only ever been undergraduate students, they see themselves as the center of the system. But they’re really the compensatory engine of a system that is producing something that is actually not their education. I think that is fascinating. I truly care so much about my students. My students are the reason I want to be in academia, but for many researchers and faculty members, students are not the reason that they are doing their job.

    It has been revealed that AC: Also, the people who run the college, the board and the President, they’re looking at the bottom line. There’s this question that’s the propulsive engine of the first act: Is Basin College going to close? Celia cares because of the archive and because it’s her home. But there’s also the question of what about all of these students that are currently there. What’s going to happen to them?

    Sources indicate that there is this unspoken understanding that the board doesn’t care about them. It’s not about them. They’re a part of this system and nobody is thinking about them at all.

    AD: They’re running a business.

    According to recent reports, RB: The book was coming out of a moment when it felt like universities were operating as these hedge funds for the wealthy. We started writing this book in 2023. Now higher education is under threat. I think that the university is a really good and key thing in our society. I want to defend it and I want to be a good voice in the university.

    AC: I think there’s a substantial question in the book, “how do you love something?” Celia’s version of loving it is excusing any of its wrongs and pretending it’s perfect. Harriot’s version is critiquing it almost to the point of picking it apart.

    I think that’s how we feel about the university. Yes, it’s wonderful. It’s something that we need. It also is worthy of critique and could be improved and made better. There are these questions of how you engage with something that you love, and because you love it you are frustrated by it greatly.

    AD: Historically most universities were set apart from cities to let people study and work. And there’s a way that attracts people like Celia who use it as a place to hide from the larger world.

    It has been revealed that RB: It’s got a monastic quality. That can also go into a cult-like quality. Harriot is really running from her past by arriving at Basin College, which is a very particularly isolated and spooky version.

    AD: It is very remote, but also, there are a lot of colleges in the middle of nowhere.

    AC: Beatrice Donahue created it specifically for that reason. She said, “my husband is finally dead, I have money, I am free. I want to go do exactly what I want to do.”.

    What she wanted to do was find some place remote where she and the women in her life and her lover could be themselves in all of their weird, witchy, queer glory. A lot of universities were not created for that reason, but it was fun to think about this university that was and how these things can start from such a seed and still become so institutionalized and twisted and different from the starting place.

    In a recent development, RB: I do like that point that Basin College in its foundational message, was meant to be a safe place for women and a safe place for queer people to live as their true selves. I feel like the university can be that way. The ivory tower is a place where you see many different kinds of people getting to ask the kinds of questions they’re interested in. I feel like that is a beautiful thing about college. But it all depends on who’s in charge.

    AD: It does get at that, which is so notable for people. Also it touches on how a lot of schools that may have become institutions, but were started by people who were strange or even crazy.

    Industry observers note that AC: [laughs] Beatrice is, but she’s gloriously powerful. She’s dead but she has cast such a long shadow. She brought these women who did not fit in society. One of our inspirations was Victorian tea rooms, which was one of the few jobs back then that women could have. So Beatrice had a tea room. Women were finding ways to exist and to be free under incredible constraints. That’s what Basin College was for her.

    In a recent development, AD: It’s a queer book about how queer spaces have always existed just as queer people have always existed. And that these spaces and institutions have existed through time.

    RB: This is our third novel and in our previous work we’ve had queer storylines that have been a reclaiming of queer joy, which has been really wonderful. In this book we wanted to just have freaky scary lesbians doing bad things and not apologizing for it. Just ripping the world down.

    AC: There’s all sorts of different ways that queer people can be portrayed. Because they’re people. You almost have to start with a portrayal where they are good, because there are a lot of people that may not have knowingly met a queer person. You almost have to start with, guess what, you can love a queer character. The more these stories come out, the more freedom you have to add grittiness and reality into that portrayal.

    It’s wonderful to be able to have queer characters that behave badly and it doesn’t feel like a condemnation on queerness as an entire experience. For us, being able to write through queer joy gave us the freedom to write queer messiness as well.

    RB: This is coming from our background as Southern women, as well. I feel like up in these parts it can feel that queer pain is a distant memory for many people, but for us, coming out in 2018 was a completely different world. Writing Southern stories about queer people means a lot to people in Arkansas and these places.

    AC: There’s people that would have you believe that queerness doesn’t exist there. Or that it needs to be kept very quiet, or regulated extremely heavily. Or made illegal. But there have always been queer people in Arkansas.

    There’s also the idea that the North is the home of the ivory tower. That Fresh England is where you’ve got all these schools, but there’s always been incredible intelligence like in Arkansas. These things, that they would have you believe don’t exist, have always been there. These people, that they tell you don’t exist or don’t deserve to exist, have always been there and been a part of it.

    AD: As you were talking about the messiness, I keep thinking about how the book takes place over a few months. It opens with the fall semester and the school is functioning as it has been, and by the Christmas holiday, everything unravels and descends into chaos.

    In a recent development, RB: We have Beatrice Donahue’s dark secret at the center of the novel. You don’t find out right away, which has made it hard for me at times to know how to pitch the novel. I feel like this is a key element that you don’t want to spoil. Beatrice lost her lover and the aftermath of that grief and where she goes with that is super kinky and interesting and transgressive and queer.

    It has been revealed that then you have these women in the 1980s that are excavating that and discovering within themselves how they feel about that and how they feel about each other. It’s fun to surprise the reader with that part way through. It’s good to highlight for readers that the book is spicy and bizarre. And a great time, hopefully.

    According to recent reports, AC:  We’re thinking about all of these highfalutin ideas, but we’re also playing a game of chicken with each other. We’re trying to freak each other out a little bit when we’re writing. We’re trying to make it fun.

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes I write something and then I’m sitting there waiting for Robin to get to it so I can get her reaction. There’s a lot about the book that is intentionally fun because we were having fun. Everything that the reader feels, we felt as we were writing it and surprising each other and grossing each other out and delighting each other.

    According to recent reports, AD: I’m sure. Going, what if she cuts her foot, what if it gets infected, what if we have this body horror scene.

    It has been revealed that AC: What’s weird is that we wrote all of that, but it grosses me out to think about it. One of my friends was reminding me about a particular scene with the foot. I remember us writing that, and I have not gone back and read it again because it grosses me out! [laughs].

    AD: I’m pretty sure I know the exact scene you’re talking about.

    AC: [laughs] It’s a weird way to feel about something you wrote.

    AD: At the center of the book is this lost manuscript of Beatrice’s, and in writing the book you had to figure out how much of that book to write, how much to include so it doesn’t overwhelm the story.

    Sources indicate that AC: A couple people have asked about this, actually. One friend said, “you should do Dreams of the Rose, the entire book from Beatrice Donahue.” Our answer has consistently been, “no!” My gosh, that was so hard to do.

    In a recent development, RB: One of the significant influences in the book that I don’t think we’ve talked about before is Possession by A.S. Byatt. I love that novel. It’s absolutely amazing. In that book there’s a lot of the writing of the authors in the book.

    With Beatrice Donahue we wanted the kind of unreachability of her to be center stage. What’s on the page is all of the writings of Beatrice Donahue that there is. There’s no additional pages. We found it extremely tiresome to do.

    Industry observers note that harriot has this power of mimicry where she can hear the writing of someone else and then produce it. That came from my own perception of my own writing. I feel like I can really get the sound of someone else’s writing and copy that or produce that, in a sense. Beatrice Donahue is a shared character, but I would read Mary Shelley and Poe and nineteenth-century work and then I would write these passages of Donahue.

    I’m very attuned to word choice. I feel like it’s so easy to get taken out of that kind of writing with a misplaced word or something that just doesn’t hit quite right. This is just someone in the present pretending to write about the past. I wanted it to have a strong truth claim. Starting with the note from the editors and then all the writing, I wanted it to feel really immersive. This could have been true.

    AD: You mentioned before that each were the primary writer of one of the characters. Who did you write?

    AC: I wrote Celia. To the great surprise of most people, I wrote Celia.

    RB: For some reason, Alex’s friends were like, “she couldn’t have done that.”.

    AC: I think because the wildness of Celia and where we go in her perspective is pretty stark. I think that a lot of people that know me are just surprised because I’m an introvert. There’s a lot that comes out in Celia’s perspective that people maybe didn’t think we were capable of, who have read our other books or know us personally.

    AD: I think Celia would have to be written by an introvert.

    AC: That’s how I feel! She’s got a very rich inner world, and it’s twisted in there.

    AD: It’s also funny that you wrote the foot scene and then went, this is disgusting, I can’t read it again.

    RB: Alex writes way grosser stuff than I do.

    AD: That is interesting. Do people have a somewhat misunderstood sense of what you write or how you write?

    RB: I think there’s definitely a pattern between the three books. Alex’s characters are always extremely vulnerable and very emotionally open. Which is interesting because between the two of us, she’s definitely more emotionally unavailable in the real world. My characters are a bit more closed off and they’re usually cool. [laughs] I’m the least cool person, but then I write these cool characters. To my best friends, it’s pretty obvious that Harriot is me. She’s like my shadow side.

    Recent findings suggest that people do have a good time guessing. We go back and forth, should we tell people who wrote what? Should we keep it a secret? Because obviously we want the experience to be seamless.

    AD: You mentioned one struggle has been finding a way to talk about the book without spoiling too much. Which I understand.

    It has been revealed that RB: I’ve been thinking about the pitch for the book and if we’re pitching it correctly. I think what it’s really about is that Celia longs for more than anything, the love of this Victorian author that she’s always admired. In her desperate reaching for that, she recruits her academic nemesis who has this talent for mimicry to go with her on this journey that leads to a total shit show descent into complete chaos in this snowy remote college.

    In a recent development, that’s what I think the book is about. There’s many, many bizarre and spicy surprises along the way. [laughs].

    AD: It’s true, and a lot of what we’ve been talking about, the gothic elements and academia and the two falling for each other, that’s the first half. The second half, just buckle up for the ride.

    RB: Someone asked us, do you provide aftercare for your readers at the end of the book? I was like, we don’t. I feel like the book is just like a rock and roll roller coaster and you get spat out at the end. I hope that you’re sitting there, staring at the book going, what did I just read? [laughs].

    #136934. David Brandon Hodge on occult murders and the origins of Ouija boards

    David Brandon Hodge on occult murders and the origins of Ouija boards

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At the time of the New Planchette article’s circulation in 1886, Charles Kennard was a real estate agent who owned a fertilizer business in Chestertown, Maryland, just across the wide expanse of the Chesapeake Bay from the state’s industrial center of Baltimore. Kennard was born in Delaware on Christmas Eve, 1857, and was eleven years old when he witnessed the “wonderful workings of Planchette” during its ﬁrst great craze. By 1876, he had begun “an investigation of psychical phenomenon” while living in Philadelphia, and his table-rapping experiments continued after he moved to Chestertown that same year.

    While Kennard never acknowledged any inﬂuence of the Ohio talking-board reports that appeared in 1886, it was that same year he claimed he envisioned an identical breakthrough, imagining he could receive communications quicker than raps or automatic writing “if words could be spelled by the alphabet.” He struck on what he believed was an original idea: “In 1886 I made a crude board, using a cake board and a table with four legs and a pointer, marking the alphabet and numerals in pencil,” and used the pairing to autonomously spell out messages letter by letter, joining the ranks of Armstrong, Damon, and Long as one of the earliest- known talking-board creators.

    In a recent development, to reﬁne his primitive eﬀorts, Kennard claimed, he visited local cabinetmaker and undertaker Ernest Christian “E. C.” Reiche, a Prussian immigrant whose workshop was adjacent to Kennard’s oﬃce in Chestertown’s Voshell House. He commissioned “about a dozen boards a little neater in appearance than the cake board,” which he then oﬀered for sale locally. He claimed his boards were “always being borrowed by neighbors, and those who purchased the few wanted more,” echoing similar stirrings of interest in Ohio that same year.

    By his own account, he petitioned Reiche to continue the productive partnership, but as Kennard later recalled, “I asked him to continue making them for me and we would put the board on the market. This he noted he would not do. He was too busy to make any more. I would have to get someone else.” Left without a craftsman to manufacture the boards, Kennard’s commercial ambitions sat temporarily idle.

    Recent findings suggest that three years later, a competitive marketplace took its toll on Kennard’s fertilizer business, and in February 1890, he relocated his family to Baltimore. There, he opened a newly introduced real estate oﬃce in the Barnum Building and established new headquarters for his fertilizer company at 220 S. Charles Street. Kennard also rekindled his ambition to commercialize a talking board.10 In an account that echoes Cyrus H. Farley’s attempts to pitch planchettes in Boston, Kennard “showed the board to several who could see nothing of the future in it.”.

    But a fortuitous meeting came with local attorney and fellow Freemason Elijah Jeﬀerson Bond, who took an intense interest in what he called Kennard’s “witch board.” Bond recounted in later years how he made “important improvements” to Kennard’s design to get it into “marketable shape,” which included a round planchette with a sharply pointed extension that served as an indicator, setting it far apart from the heart-shaped planchettes of yesteryear. He paired the new planchette with a board that included two arched rows of the alphabet with a straight line of numbers below, closely matching newspaper illustrations from 1886.

    Bond added embellishments, including a black dot representing the full moon in one upper corner and a crescent moon in the other, and black stars in the bottom corners. An illustration at the bottom center depicting two men shaking hands—an crucial symbol of fraternity among Freemasons—ﬂanked on each side with the conjunction “Good Bye.”.

    The pair partnered with the goal of patenting and manufacturing the idea, with Bond ﬁnancing their earliest eﬀorts with a $500 investment.

    According to recent reports, the duo’s new talking board had not yet been christened with its iconic name. As the two ironed out the details of the patent design in April 1890, they assembled at Bond’s home with some of his family members. Not satisﬁed with the initial name they had chosen, Charles Kennard proposed they ask the board what it would like to be called, as he later recounted:.

    The name Ouija was adopted by Mr. Bond and myself. We called this board by another name until we could secure a better one. One evening about April 1890, while trying the board with a Miss Peters, Mr. Bond’s sister-in-law, in the large boarding house at that time on the corner of Charles and Centre streets, where Mr. Bond boarded, I remarked that we had not yet settled upon a name, and as the board had helped us in other ways, we would ask it to propose one. It spelled out O-U-I-J-A. When I asked the meaning of the word it stated “Good Luck.”.

    In a recent development, miss Peters there upon drew upon her neck a chain which had at the end a locket, on it a ﬁgure of a woman and at the top the word “Ouija.” We asked her if she had thought of the name, and she remarked she had not. We then adopted the word.

    It has been revealed that ouija was a strange word seemingly without precedent, and its fascinating combination of consonants and vowels, fabricated through Peters’s mediumship, added to the board’s mystique, even as unlikely as it was to have appeared on a locket. Yet her locket is an key clue that her role in Ouija’s naming may have direct ties to the Spiritualist movement.

    It has been revealed that peters had no known connection to Spiritualism in her upbringing, but such influence was deeply rooted in her future husband and then suitor Ernest Herbert Donisthorpe Nosworthy. An immigrant from the UK who arrived in January 1888 to work as a traveling salesman, Nosworthy was the seventh child of Frederick Arthur and Eliza Louisa Spry Nosworthy, née Thompson, of Manchester, England, the latter of whom was a talented trance medium who “often attracted large and refined public audiences at Birkenhead by her dramatic powers.”.

    She was the daughter of George Thompson, himself a prominent Spiritualist who sat with Leah Fox in the United States, and had served on the Council of the British National Association of Spiritualists. The younger Nosworthy’s sister, Beatrice, was also regarded as “one of the youngest and one of the best of trance mediums” in England.

    The Nosworthy family’s close bonds with one of the most famous mediums of the era may have directly influenced Ouija’s name. The family hosted famous medium Cora Hatch when she visited England, living with them for months at a time on multiple occasions during Nosworthy’s formative school years. Eliza Nosworthy was considered Hatch’s herald and was so close to the family that when Eliza’s prominent father died, the medium adopted him as a new spirit guide with the blessing of the Nosworthy clan.

    However, it was another of Hatch’s spirit guides who might have inspired Ouija’s name: the specter of a woman named Ouina, Cora Scott’s most famous contact for her trance mediumship, and Spiritualists considered her a generous spirit who acted as “a messenger of peace and love between the two worlds.” Exposure to Ouina was most certainly in the environment of Ernest Nosworthy’s upbringing, and it may explain the mysterious locket with a woman’s figure and name described by Kennard in his remembrance of Ouija’s naming.

    Whatever the case, Bond and Kennard adopted the enigmatic moniker and turned toward securing a patent for their newly named product.

    During the mid-1930s, more stories of deaths involving messages received through Ouija made the headlines of American newspapers. The first involved the Turley family of Arizona, when fifteen-year-old Mattie shot her father, Ernes, twice in the back with a shotgun, which resulted in his death a few weeks later.

    According to recent reports, the news spread far beyond local publications when reports revealed that it was Ouija’s messages that had commanded Mattie to murder her father. The story was further sensationalized by news that her mother and Ernest’s wife, Dorothea, was once voted “the most beautiful girl in America.”.

    It has been revealed that widely reprinted articles revealed how Dorothea had become obsessed with a local “handsome cowboy” named Kent Pearce and used the Ouija to manipulate her daughter into murdering her own father so that Dorothea would be free to marry Pearce. All three were charged, although Pearce denied any involvement and was ultimately found not guilty. Mattie pled guilty in juvenile court and was sentenced to an Arizona reform school, while her mother was found guilty and sentenced to prison but was freed three years later.

    Sources indicate that another sensational Ouija murder involved the Hurd family of Kansas City in 1935. Family matriarch Nellie received messages through her Ouija that her seventy-seven-year-old husband, Herbert, was “too fond of another woman” and that he had given his secret lover “$15,000 of a hidden fortune.”.

    After receiving the messages, Nellie and her daughter Bertha ambushed Herbert and chained him to his bed before subjecting him to all manner of tortures, including beating him with a revolver, burning the soles of his feet with matches, and stabbing his legs with a dagger. Bertha also set to killing “the children”—three dogs and a cat—with carbon monoxide, which Nellie had commanded.

    These horrible acts led to Herbert signing a forced confession admitting to his affair, which the two women signed as “witnesses.” But a few hours later, Nellie momentarily left her gun within Herbert’s reach, and he seized it and shot his wife four times before making his escape.

    Police afterward discovered Herbert “running along the street clad only in his pajamas and carrying a still smoking revolver,” and he confessed to police immediately. Nellie died from her wounds, and the courts deter-mined her death to be a “justifiable homicide.” Bertha remained free after Herbert refused to press charges.

    As in prior decades, these Ouija-inspired murders sparked a flurry of sensational headlines like “The Ouija Again Spelled Death!” even if Herbert’s actions were an act of self-defense, and helped contribute to the growing chorus of Ouija’s malign and diabolical associations in the media.

    Recent findings suggest that david Brandon Hodge is the author ofSupernatural Machines: The History of Spirit Communication Devices. Hodge is a historian, collector, and author specializing in the history of spirit communication devices. Founder of MysteriousPlanchette.com and curator of the world’s largest archive of séance artifacts, his research has appeared in Smithsonian Magazine and Paranormal Review, and has served as a consultant for museums and exhibitions worldwide, including the acclaimed Supernatural America exhibit at the Minneapolis Institute of Art and the Peabody Essex Museum’s Conjuring the Spirit World exhibit. Hodge has also appeared in many prominent programs as an expert on the occult, including Oddities, Mysteries at the Museum, and Expedition Files, and served as historical consultant and provided séance artifacts for Rick Alverson’s film The Mountain and Lasse Hellström’s biopic Hilma. Hodge is also a respected game designer and lecturer, known for his horror-themed scenarios and his work with Atlas Obscura and Coast to Coast AM. He owns and operates Monkey See, Monkey Do! toy store and Substantial Top Candy Shop in Austin, Texas, where he lives with his two children, Jack and Elliot, and the ghosts of several cats.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Taormina is a ruthless condemnation of our selfish modern era, a road trip novel in which a married couple on vacation in Italy run over a migrant child, then proceed to do….nothing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that here are five newly translated works of crime fiction, featuring selfish tourists, corrupt cops, desperate horse racers, antiquities smugglers, and amateur sleuths. Enjoy!

    Yves Ravey, Taormina Translated by Alyson Waters (Newly introduced York Review of Books).

    Taormina is a ruthless condemnation of our selfish modern era, a road trip novel in which a married couple on vacation in Italy run over a migrant child, then proceed to do….nothing. They do not check on the body. They do not go to the police. They do not accept any form of responsibility. They don’t even bother to cover up their crimes (or at least, they cover for themselves only lazily and ineptly). The only action available to either spouse, by dint of their warped world view, is to blame others for their problems. A vicious gem that wouldn’t feel out of place in mid-century noir, although the story’s catalysts are firmly grounded in the 21st century.

    Gustavo Eduardo Abrevaya, The Bullet Inside Me Translated by Andrea G Labinger ( Schaffner Press).

    Recent findings suggest that the Bullet Inside Me takes places at the height of Argentina’s Secret War; in this hard-boiled thriller of compromise and conspiracy, the young daughter of a fascist functionary is kidnapped, in a case that threatens the entire dictatorial order. By the same author as the impressive Sanctuary, this one’s just as compelling, and just as vicious.

    Genki Kawamura, The Horse and I Translated by Chikako Kobayashi (Flatiron).

    A beautiful tale of the lengths we go to for love. In The Horse and Me, a shy clerk forges a deep bond with a racing horse, one coveted by a wealthy rider who seems poised to destroy the stallion’s spirit. Without means of her own, the clerk begins stealing from her own union’s coffers in order to purchase, then maintain, her newfound soulmate. When her colleagues begin to catch on to the thefts, Kawamura’s heroine finds herself backed into a corner and desperate to turn her horse into a champion.

    Sacha Naspini, The Witch’s Mouth Translated by Clarissa Botsford  (Europa).

    Grave robbing in Tuscany from ancient Etruscan graves has been substantial business since before the war, but with fresh regulations cracking down on antiquities smuggling elsewhere in Italy, the little band of thieves at the center of the novel face new gangs trying to muscle into their territory, renewed inquiries from weary local authorities, and internal divisions that threaten to dissolve their operation entirely.

    Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press).

    It has been revealed that hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

    Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

    The U.S. Navy is retiring the peacoat—the kind that Robert Redford wore in Three Days of the Condor

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to The Fashion Police, a column where we spotlight some of the best fashion in crime film and TV.
    • The United States navy is retiring a its signature peacoat.
    • Industry observers note that they are replacing it with a black, synthetic, all-weather parka.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to The Fashion Police, a column where we spotlight some of the best fashion in crime film and TV.

    In a recent development, it’s true. The United States navy is retiring a its signature peacoat. Yes, its signature peacoat! “The double-breasted, hip-length wool peacoat that is synonymous with the romance of the sea.” They’re retiring an iconic garment, a staple not only of military fashion, but also of fashion in general.

    Industry observers note that they are replacing it with a black, synthetic, all-weather parka. Why are they doing this? A statement from the Navy’s Uniform Board said that it was due to the Navy’s “commitment to eliminating unnecessary costs while ensuring sailors have the cold-weather protection they need to accomplish their missions.” The U.S. Naval Institute News revealed that it was chosen was chosen for its “modern appearance,” and “its versatility in being able to be worn with service and dress uniforms and civilian clothing.” But it has NO personality. This is like tearing down a historic 18th century townhouse to put up a glass and steel high rise.

    In her piece on this landmark decision, Vanessa Friedman at The New York Times noted the history and symbolic associations of the garment, writing.

    According to recent reports, first designed for Dutch sailors in the 18th century, the pijakker was particularly well-suited for life at sea: roomy enough to accommodate warm inner layers but streamlined enough not to get caught in a ship’s rigging. Its collar could be turned up to shield the face against wind, and side pockets kept the coat closer to the body in cold weather.

    Adopted by the Royal Navy in 1857, the peacoat made the leap to the U.S. Navy shortly thereafter, becoming standard issue in 1886. And though small details may have been tweaked, the general style has remained the same.

    Sources indicate that in 1962, Friedman notes, Yves Saint-Laurent included a peacoat in his womenswear Rive-Gauche show, launching the coat as as style staple for women. According to the brand,.

    The simple shape of this practical garment sculpted the silhouette. The fact that it was not fitted and covered the hips made it ideal for women who did not yet feel daring enough to wear pants, which accentuated the female form.

    Saint Laurent’s 1962 fashion show opened with the pea coat, which was the first piece he presented under his own name. The model wore it with white shantung pants and mules. This ensemble paved the way for Yves Saint Laurent’s signature style, which borrowed from menswear in order to make women feel comfortable and confident.

    According to recent reports, but, for our purposes, the most iconic use of the peacoat is Robert Redford’s look in Three Days of the Condor, Sydney Pollack’s 1975 political espionage thriller, based on James Grady’s novel Six Days of the Condor). Redford plays a low-level CIA employee in New York City who is the sole survivor of an attack on his small office branch, and then goes on the run, attempting to untangle what appears to be an enormous intra-bureau conspiracy. The peacoat is a nice choice for this character; as Valerie Steele, the director of the Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology told The New York Times, “the peacoat doesn’t have the associations with violence and warfare often attached to camouflage and Army greatcoats. Rather, the peacoat more often represents bravery against the elements and the romance of voyages to places unknown.”.

    Sources indicate that olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Second District Court Rules Against Trump's Latest Birthright Citizenship Executive Order

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that yesterday, in the case of Nathan v.
    • Recent findings suggest that I previously  wrote about Trump's new executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it.
    • Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the upcoming order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that yesterday, in the case of Nathan v. Trump, federal district Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of DC issued a ruling against Trump's upcoming executive order restricting birthright citizenship. The ruling is very similar to an earlier September decision by Judge Boardman of the District of Maryland. The one difference is that the class action injunction in Nathan covers a class that literally consists of all children illegally deprived of birthright citizenship under the new order, whereas the class in the Maryland case is slightly narrower.

    Recent findings suggest that I previously  wrote about Trump's new executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to various classes of children born on US soil, and noted the first legal challenges to it. As I pointed out then, almost every part of the new order is at odds with the Supreme Court's recent ruling in Trump v. Barbara, which struck down Trump's executive order denying birthright citizenship to children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States, and those born to non-citizen parents here on temporary visas. The Fourteenth Amendment guarantees citizenship to all children "born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof." In Barbara, the Supreme Court majority made clear that "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" includes children of all persons who are subject to and required to obey US law.

    Judge Cooper rightly concludes that nearly all the various classes of children barred from birthright citizenship by the upcoming order are in fact protected by the reasoning of Barbara and other Supreme Court precedents, because they and their parents are clearly subject to US law, and required to obey it:.

    Earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's Executive Order 14160, which purported to deny citizenship to children born to parents temporarily or unlawfully present in the country. Those children, like "nearly all children born in the United States," the Court explained, are "citizens at birth" because they are born "subject to American law." Trump v. Barbara, 609 U.S. 719, 734–37, 740–41 (2026). Barbara reaffirmed that birthright citizenship extends to all but three narrow categories of children, each long understood to be beyond the Nation's governing authority at birth: children of foreign officials enjoying full diplomatic immunity, children of enemy forces in hostile occupation of U.S. territory, and children born aboard foreign public ships.

    Yet Barbara's ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at matter here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents. Among those now targeted are children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organizations but lack diplomatic immunity, children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements, and children with a parent suspected of membership in certain gangs or terrorist organizations. As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out latest exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws. The Court will therefore certify a class consisting of children who are or will be unlawfully denied citizenship under the Order. And it will preliminarily enjoin the Government from enforcing the Order against members of that class.

    As explained in my original August post on the fresh executive order, that order covers four groups almost all of whose members are clearly subject to US law:.

    Recent findings suggest that children of "alien enemies," defined as those where at least one of two non-citizen parents is a "designated Foreign Terrorist Organization under 8 U.S.C. 1189 or Specially Designated Global Terrorist, consistent with the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq., and Executive Order 13224 of September 23, 2001 (Blocking Property and Prohibiting Transactions With Persons Who Commit, Threaten to Commit, or Support Terrorism).".

    Children born to at least one non-citizen parent who is a "foreign government employee" or employed by an "international organization that possess[es] international-organization immunity.".

    Children where "either parent" has engaged in "birth tourist" transactions of various kinds (deliberately seeking to give birth in the US so the child would get birthright citizenship).

    Children "born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute." …[T]his only applies to children born in American Samoa, the one populated overseas US territory to whose residents Congress has not conferred citizenship by statute….

    As I explained more fully in my August post, all of the children in these four categories are obviously subject to US law, with the exception of those born to foreign diplomats who have diplomatic immunity. This latter group is already excluded from birthright citizenship. In that post, I also explained why the analogy between "alien enemies" (as defined in the order) and children of members of an invading army occupying US territory fails.

    Recent findings suggest that judge Cooper's opinion analyzes all four categories thoroughly and effectively. He's particularly strong on the case of children of "alien enemies," a category which - he explains - the Trump order defines far more broadly than is justified by legal precedent, and which in any case does not include anyone not "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States, because all such people are under US control and required to obey US law when on American soil. That differentiates them from the historically recognized exception for children of enemy troops in "hostile occupation" of US territory during a war. The US does not have effective jurisdiction over territory occupied by a hostile enemy army. But the last time any such thing occurred was during World War II, when the Japanese occupied a number of US island possessions in the Pacific.

    I noted some additional problems with Trump's "alien enemies" carveout in my August post about the second birthright citizenship order:.

    It has been revealed that finally, the [order is wrong about] children of "alien enemies," defined…. as members of various designated "terrorist" entities. If they enter the United States, they are subject to US law. That's why they can be prosecuted for any crimes they commit on US soil - including acts of terrorism!

    Members of these groups may be bad people. Some have committed horrendous crimes. But that is no reason to visit the sins of the parents upon the children. If a murderer or a rapist has a child born on US soil, the child is entitled to birthright citizenship, notwithstanding the reprehensible behavior of the parents. The same logic applies here.

    It is also worth noting that the "foreign terrorist organization" (FTO) designation has been slapped onto various groups that are not actually terrorists in the ordinary meaning of the word, most notably groups engaged in smuggling illegal drugs.

    In a recent development, trump may be trying to use the "alien enemy" designation here to analogize these children to children of members of an invading army, born  at a time and place where the invaders have seized control of US territory, thereby preventing the exercise of US "jurisdiction." Trump v. Barbara reaffirms the longstanding view that such children are excluded from birthright citizenship, because born in an area where US jurisdiction does not (at the time) meaningfully apply.

    Recent findings suggest that but FTOs have not, in fact, "invaded" or occupied any part of the United States. Thus, US jurisdiction still applies. Therefore, children of members these organizations are not analogous to children born to members of an occupying foreign army. No part of the United States has actually been invaded and occupied since the Japanese seized various US territories in the Pacific during World War II.

    In my article, "Immigration is Not Invasion….," I explain in much more detail why the activities of drug dealers do not qualify as an "invasion," why an FTO designation cannot change that reality, and why courts should not defer to the president's claims that an "invasion" has occurred.
