    #136921. Breaking: Jessica Hamilton on possession, menopause, and the horrors of middle age

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1197 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Jessica Hamilton on possession, menopause, and the horrors of middle age

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that demonic possession or plain old menopause?
    • According to recent reports, in my novel, The Woods, my protagonist, Alice, is in the throes of middle age.
    • Recent findings suggest that scalding flames spread quickly up the chest, wrapping a burning hand around the neck, moving onto the face causing a sheen of sweat on the forehead and upper lip that only intensifies the burn—no escape is possible from the fire within.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that demonic possession or plain old menopause? It can be hard to tell, which is why the horrors of middle age for women lend themselves so well to the horror genre. There are the physical horrors, when our bodies betray us. There are the psychological ones, when our minds betray us. And there are the sociological ones, perhaps the most insidious of them all, when our own communities betray us.

    According to recent reports, in my novel, The Woods, my protagonist, Alice, is in the throes of middle age. So, while she’s sure something sinister is in the woods, which seems to be targeting her family, she also questions herself at every turn, is constantly doubted by those around, her all while powering through the many physical hurdles of menopause.

    Recent findings suggest that scalding flames spread quickly up the chest, wrapping a burning hand around the neck, moving onto the face causing a sheen of sweat on the forehead and upper lip that only intensifies the burn—no escape is possible from the fire within. A description of an everyday hot flash and yet it reads like a scene in a horror novel of a person being burned alive. The same can be done for the rivers of blood that may run unabated, the headaches that feel like a metal stake being driven into the scalp, the withering of the skin, the clumps of hair found in the drain after showering, the crack and creak of joints that ache.

    These physical symptoms sound like well-known body horror tropes but are in fact real life experiences for many women going through menopause. In combination these symptoms can easily make a woman feel as though her body has been possessed by some evil force.

    In his novel, Mary, Nat Cassidy describes the physical struggles of his middle-aged protagonist, Mary, in such a visceral way that it is in itself the horror. Making the reader forget that this is a stage of life that all women go through and not just the fiction of a very adept horror author.

    Then there are the psychological impacts of middle age for women. Extreme fatigue, anxiety, unprovoked anger, incessant mental chatter, dark thoughts, disrupted sleep, sudden surges of unmanageable rage, untreatable depression, gaps in memory—I have heard many women complain of one or more of these symptoms due to menopause.

    According to recent reports, and yet, this list is what comes up when you google the symptoms of demonic possession. Clearly making the point that middle age lends itself well to the horror novel. It is one thing to feel that your body is turning on you, it’s another to feel that your mind is as well. And if you can’t trust yourself, then who can you trust?

    Industry observers note that in the novel, Death in Her Hands by Ottessa Moshfegh the protagonist Vesta becomes obsessed with a note that she finds in the woods around her house and the mystery that it presents. Very rapidly the lines of reality become blurred for Vesta due to her confused state and her inability to decipher what is real and what is her own paranoia and delusion. She can’t trust herself which means she’s locked in an inescapable cycle of discovering something and then mistrusting that discovery.

    According to recent reports, my own protagonist, Alice, senses that there is something sinister in the woods around their latest home but is prone to second guessing her own intuition because she no longer feels as sure of her memory or perception as she once did, before middle age. She wants to assert herself and what she believes is happening but lacks the confidence to do so under the influence of menopause.

    If you’re unable to trust your memory, if you’re prone to paranoia and anxiety, irrational mood swings and brain fog you’re also ripe to be gaslit by those around you. Women being gaslit is not a latest concept. The diagnosis of hysteria, which women were given until it was removed from the DSM in1980, was perhaps the most powerful tool of gaslighting.

    According to recent reports, these days it’s a little less obvious but happens just the same. It’s easy to dismiss a middle-aged women’s feelings by claiming that they are caused my menopausal hormones. But, if the paranoia, anxiety, depression grief etc. are in fact rooted in something other than hormonal changes this leaves a woman without the support she actually needs.

    In a recent development, in the case of my protagonist, her concerns about the safety of her family and the threat of the woods are dismissed by her husband, mother and best friend as the ramblings of a paranoid, anxiety riddled, grief stricken menopausal woman. Add to this the fact that women often feel invisible in society after reaching middle age and it results in lack of credibility, power and presence. What could be worse than the horror of not being believed, not having any authority and not being seen?

    According to recent reports, why did I choose to write about a middle-aged woman experiencing menopause in my latest novel? I’m fifty-one years old and have begun to experience a lot of what my protagonist, Alice, experiences. I wanted to give a voice to this stage in life and hopefully create some empathy for it in readers.

    According to recent reports, mostly though, it was because the things that Alice was experiencing at this stage of life were great tools to ramp up the tension of the horror in my writing. A character filled with paranoia, anxiety, and sleeplessness from the very start of the novel. One who questions herself and is questioned by those around her and who causes the reader to question whether something is real or simply a paranoid delusion. Set this character in a house with a tragic history, surrounded by ancient woods and I was off to the races.

    It has been revealed that the simple truth is that often real life is the scariest of all and in the case of middle age for women, I’m sad to say, that is most certainly the case. Demonic possession or menopause? My bet is that it’s menopause. I don’t believe in demons, despite being a writer of horror.

    In a recent development, fortunately, there’s hormone replacement therapy, an increase in information about it and the horror does, apparently, have an end at some point. In the meantime, may there be many more novels that have the menopausal hero saving the day, despite the hot flashes, brain fog, sleepless nights and gaslighting.

    Jessica Hamilton was born in Australia but grew up in Canada. She has lived and worked in the Czech Republic, Taiwan, India and Japan. She studied writing at the Humber School for Writers as well as George Brown College. She lives in Ontario, Canada with her husband, son and daughter. Her debut novel is titled What You Never Knew, her second novel is titled, Don't You Dare, and both are thrillers published by Crooked Lane Books.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This month’s recommendations feature Zhang Yimou’s sumptuous story of organized crime in 1930s Shanghai; Sergei Loznitsa’s disturbing satire set in Russian-occupied Ukraine; and Manuella Martinelli’s quietly haunting depiction of Augusto Pinochet’s Chile.
    • According to recent reports, with Gong Li (Memoirs of A Geisha, Farewell My Concubine) in the lead role as Bijou, a nightclub singer and the mistress of an underworld boss (Li Boatian), Zhang Yimou’s Shanghai Triad features opulent period sets and a propulsive narrative.
    • Over the course of seven days, Shuisheng learns about those rules as he witnesses gangland shootouts, discovers that Bijou is having an affair, and watches as Bijou’s relationship with the Boss unravels in intrigue and betrayal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This month’s recommendations feature Zhang Yimou’s sumptuous story of organized crime in 1930s Shanghai; Sergei Loznitsa’s disturbing satire set in Russian-occupied Ukraine; and Manuella Martinelli’s quietly haunting depiction of Augusto Pinochet’s Chile.

    Glamorous, criminal underworld,1930s Shanghai.

    According to recent reports, with Gong Li (Memoirs of A Geisha, Farewell My Concubine) in the lead role as Bijou, a nightclub singer and the mistress of an underworld boss (Li Boatian), Zhang Yimou’s Shanghai Triad features opulent period sets and a propulsive narrative. The story unfolds from the perspective of 14-year old Shuisheng (Wang Xiao Xiao) who has been sent from the countryside by his uncle to work for the Boss, who in turn makes him a personal servant to Bijou. “This is Shanghai,” Shuisheng is told. “There are hidden rules in everything you do or say.”.

    Over the course of seven days, Shuisheng learns about those rules as he witnesses gangland shootouts, discovers that Bijou is having an affair, and watches as Bijou’s relationship with the Boss unravels in intrigue and betrayal.

    Before making Shanghai Triad, Yimou and Li had previously collaborated on several classic films including Ju-Dou (1990) and Raise the Red Lantern (1991)—which is being re-released in theaters across North America for its thirty-fifth Anniversary.

    Directed by Zhang Yimou, 108 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    Composed of a series of several loosely linked vignettes that take place in Russian-occupied territory in Ukraine, and based on real-life amateur videos, Ukrainian director Sergei Loznitsa’s (The Two Prosecutors) Donbass makes you question everything you’re seeing. Up is down and right is wrong as actors get dressed to film what is supposed to be real news; a police chief explains to a man why his car no longer belongs to him; a bureaucrat at a maternity hospital shows staff a huge stock of food that they say they haven’t received.

    Loznitsa’s skills are on full display as he dips in and out of incidents with minimal set-up—you really don’t know where you’re headed, or what anyone will say or do—which is perhaps a good summary of what life was and is like in these zones.

    According to recent reports, filmed after Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and its covert operations in the eastern Donbass region, but before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Donbass keeps you transfixed with its bewildering and inexorable logic. In that sense, it hits too close to home. Donbass isn’t out there. It’s right here, wherever home may be. We are all living in Donbass’s world of greed, corruption, and the perversion of truth.

    Directed by Sergei Loznitsa, 122 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    In preparation for Manuella Martelli’s gripping newly introduced film, The Meltdown (2026), which releases early next year, you should watch her directorial debut, 1976 (released in the US as Chile ’76). The two films are part of a planned trilogy that explores Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship and its aftermath.

    According to recent reports, chile ’76 takes place three years after Pinochet seized power, overthrowing the democratically elected government of Salvador Allende—but none of that is top of mind for Carmen (Aline Küppenheim), a well-off middle-aged woman who heads out to her summer home to supervise renovations. In the course of her daily activities, Carmen witnesses incidents that give her pause—for instance, people on the street being dragged away—but since they don’t directly affect her, she moves on.

    According to recent reports, when a priest asks Carmen to help care for a wounded young man, she slowly discovers what’s actually happening in her country. Chile ’76 doesn’t hit you over the head with lessons about authoritarian regimes and how they operate. Instead, it reveals how even well-meaning people can turn a blind eye to violence and repression…until they can’t anymore.

    Directed by Manuella Martelli, 96 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    #136914. Wesley King: I wrote a Bloody Romantic Thriller…and I’m not even sorry

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (791 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Wesley King: I wrote a Bloody Romantic Thriller…and I’m not even sorry

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that I grew up as a nerd.
    • Sources indicate that but when romance came knocking?
    • It occurred to me that I might just like to write something romantic.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that I grew up as a nerd. Well. I also grew into a nerd. That is to say, I loved all things fantasy and science fiction, literary passions which later grew to incorporate historical fiction, murder mysteries, and heists. The Lies of Lock Lamora by Scott Lynch is a perfect example: We have magic, we have crime, this is fun.

    Sources indicate that but when romance came knocking? I needed some guidance to get started…and so I joined a reading group. I was the only man in the group, and I was pre-emptively warned that they had a predilection for smut. But, hey, I could read smut. Why not? It wasn’t just romantasy either. We ran the gauntlet. And you know what? There was some good stuff in there.

    It occurred to me that I might just like to write something romantic.

    The first question I asked myself was: Is that genre mash-up even a thing? Do thriller or crime readers want to read romance? Is an explicit sex scene going to force them to cast the book into the fire from whence it came? I didn’t know. The greatest murder mystery of all time for my money, The Murder of Roger Akroyd by Agatha Christie, didn’t have time for such frivolity.

    I knew for starters that my characters and their connection needed to feel real. That was one thing my reading group taught me: We can’t see our sexy heroes. We need an emotional runway. We need our hearts to send us a confusing memo: Wait. I could love that person.

    Recent findings suggest that so I wrote backstories. I wrote a mystery that was violent and complex and provided the twists and turns we demand in thrillers. I placed the story in smalltown Montana with significant skies and big characters: ranchers, cops, and a mysterious exile named the Hill Man. There is plenty of atmospheric horror, symbology and scares, and the ever-hanging question of whether something paranormal hangs over the mounting disappearances. I like a little Mulder in my mysteries.

    And I wrote two characters entwined in a long-doomed-romance, forever caught in each other’s orbits, and explored the way they could find their way back to each other in the pursuit of the truth. But I also leaned into it. This part wasn’t Mulder and Scully. I wanted it to feel like romance. True love and longing and lust in the midst of the carnage.

    In a recent development, so what were my lessons learned? How did I merge the genres?

    Here’s five things I did or learned through the process:.

    Sources indicate that 1. I read a shitload of genre romance.

    It has been revealed that 2. I didn’t sacrifice the fundamental aspects of crime thrillers and murder-mysteries. I built a love story in and around them.

    Industry observers note that 3. I laid off the sap. Crime and thriller readers aren’t here for I love you’s. But we do want authentic characters and dialogue, and we do have hearts buried somewhere beneath our hard-earned cynicism.

    According to recent reports, 4. The love story contributed to the plot. Yes, they have sex. But there’s a reason. And if it’s the first time you’ve read anything remotely explicit, you can say: All right, fine, not my cup of tea, but I know why we went there.

    5. Match your setting and story. Wolf Season isn’t YA. It’s also not romantasy—it’s a rough, rural crime thriller. I wanted the romance to match the setting. It’s less star-crossed lovers and more hard-boiled, cussing, and raw attraction. No one is reciting poetry. There are insults flying, guns pointed, very real danger…and two people who just can’t stay apart.

    So there you have it. I wrote a romantic thriller, and I like it. I wasn’t able to think of a clever name for the genre, so in honor of Agatha Christie, I just went across the pond with the Bloody Romantic Thriller. Feel free to use the accent.

    Sources indicate that I’ll be looking up more crossovers now, and if you’re writing a thriller or murder mystery, don’t be afraid to add a little good old-fashioned romance. Go full-on smut, if it strikes your fancy. Either way, I hope you enjoy a little romance with your murder mystery. And if not, don’t worry, there is a whole lot of shit going down in Wolf Season to buttress that hard-earned cynicism.

    • Industry observers note that most AE roles ask you to sell a product you only half understand to buyers who already know they want it.
    • If you're energized by ambiguity, allergic to bureaucracy, and the kind of seller who genuinely enjoys learning why a customer is building what they're building — keep reading.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    Industry observers note that most AE roles ask you to sell a product you only half understand to buyers who already know they want it. This is not that role. You'll sell a deeply technical product to developers, CTOs, and product teams — people who can smell a script from a mile away and will respect you more for going deep on the tech than for any closing line you've practiced. We don't have a polished playbook handed down from a head of sales who left three companies ago. We have a newly introduced sales leader, a market that's exploding faster than we can keep up with, and a real opportunity for the right person to help define the motion from the inside.

    If you're energized by ambiguity, allergic to bureaucracy, and the kind of seller who genuinely enjoys learning why a customer is building what they're building — keep reading.

    You'll thrive as an Account Executive if you:.

    are obsessed with making the best product for our customers.

    are known as the go-to person for tackling tough problems.

    work hard and can build and ship fast.

    are focused on polish, detail and quality.

    are a fast learner, frequently picking up upcoming tips, tricks, and skills.

    The best way to impress us is with thoughtful ways you'd implement LiveKit, and potentially tinkering with it 😊.

    Own and manage the full sales cycle, from prospecting and discovery to demos, negotiation, and close.

    Develop deep product understanding and communicate technical value to developers, CTOs, and product teams.

    Generate pipeline through outbound efforts and strategic partnerships, with support from marketing and sales development.

    Build and maintain strong relationships with prospects and customers, identifying their goals and how our platform helps them succeed.

    Collaborate with Product and Engineering to bring customer feedback into roadmap discussions and positioning.

    Help shape and evolve our sales playbook, messaging, and GTM motion as one of the earliest sales hires.

    Accurately forecast and track pipeline activity, working closely with leadership to inform strategy and planning.

    4+ years of full-cycle SaaS sales experience, with at least 2 of those years selling into enterprise.

    A track record of consistently selling 6-figure deals and hitting or exceeding quota in fast-paced or early-stage environments.

    Strong instincts for selling technical products — APIs, developer tools, or infrastructure tooling — you don't shy away from going deep with technical buyers.

    Comfortable in low-process, high-autonomy environments and bringing structure where it's missing.

    Able to translate technical capability into business value for both technical buyers and executive stakeholders.

    High accountability, ownership, and bias for action — you don't wait to be told what the right next move is.

    Disciplined with CRM and pipeline hygiene (HubSpot, Salesforce, etc.).

    Experience selling at an infrastructure or developer-tools organization, ideally with multi-product or platform sales motion.

    Time spent as one of the earliest sellers at a startup — you know what it feels like to build the plane while flying it.

    A real interest in voice AI, agents, or real-time infrastructure (not just "AI" in your LinkedIn headline).

    You once spent a Saturday building something with an API just to see if you could 😏.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Four days of staying in and relaxing (well, three days, if you’re cooking and/or traveling).
    • It’s a great weekend to go to the movies, You absolutely should.
    • Robert Pattinson plays Dateline journalist Chris Hansen in this thriller inspired by the developing of the To Catch a Predator segment.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ah, Thanksgiving weekend! Four days of staying in and relaxing (well, three days, if you’re cooking and/or traveling). I’ve got a suggestion about a great way to spend it, and it’s probably what you do already, this weekend, every year: catch up on recent movies!

    It’s a great weekend to go to the movies, You absolutely should. But, look, even the most intense moviegoer can’t spend the entire day, every day, at the movies. Like, even if you wanted to, the movie theater will eventually close and you’ll be forced to leave. So, there will be at least a little room for at-home viewing. And here’s what you should stream! (And go see The Only Living Pickpocket in Upcoming York in theaters!).

    Happy watching! And happy weekend!

    Robert Pattinson plays Dateline journalist Chris Hansen in this thriller inspired by the developing of the To Catch a Predator segment.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Ben Affleck directed, co-wrote, and stars in this film about a mayoral candidate and his wife who will stop at nothing to get their kidnapped son back.

    Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.

    Mahershala Ali plays a very religious hitman who must protect his children after the death of his wife.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Adria Arjona plays an army sniper/mom who winds up having to use her skills to protect her little girl from a bunch of genetically-engineered super soldiers.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Mark Wahlberg star as an FBI agent and a mob hitman who team up in 1966 to investigate the murders of several Civil Rights leaders in Mississippi.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Helen Mirren plays Patricia Highsmith in this thriller about an American man who goes Switzerland to find the legendary writer and get her to pen one last Ripley book… and he’ll go to extraordinary lengths to get her to do it.

    Streaming: Available to rent on Fandango.

    Oscar-winner Sian Heder’s upcoming film is about disability rights activist Judy Heumann’s landmark 1977 San Francisco sit-in.

    It has been revealed that wile E. Coyote, having grown frustrated with the countless ACME products that have blown up in his face, hires a personal injury attorney to sue the corporation.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    A group of smart sheep band together to investigate the murder of their beloved shepherd, who (among other things), read them mystery novels every night.

    Sources indicate that curry Barker’s surprise hit-of-the-summer is a Gen Z patch to the Monkey’s paw story. When a young man wishes that his crush will fall for him, he gets what he hopes for… but at a terrifying price.

    This sequel to Ready or Not (a movie about how Samara Weaving marries into a wealthy family, who marries into a wealthy family, only to discover that their wealth and status is the result of a devil’s bargain that requires them to occasionally sacrifice a new addition to the family in an elaborate game of “hide and seek”) picks up right after she’s made it through, when she’s challenged by a powerful group connected to her in-laws’ family (also with a Satanic pact) to a DOUBLE OR NOTHING game of hide-and-seek, and they have to play, or they’ll kill her sister.

    In Hokum, a writer travels to a hotel in an Irish village, unaware that it is haunted by a witch.

    Boots Riley’s delightful new film is about a group of shoplifters who steal from a designer, only to sell her clothes at a lower price.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Mike and Nick and Nick and Alice.

    Two gangsters in love with the same woman find themselves tested when they wind up going deep in the world of organize crime… and find their journey complicated by time travel.

    Samara Weaving and Jason Segel star as an unhappily married couple who head to a secluded cabin for a romantic getaway… but each is secretly plotting to murder the other, while they’re there.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, liveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the agentic era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe AI agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice and agentic AI applications for OpenAI, Salesforce, Spotify, Meta, and tens of thousands of other developers, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    We're hiring a Solutions Architect (Pre-Sales) to be the technical partner to the engineers and enterprises building on LiveKit.

    You'll work alongside an account executive to understand what a customer is trying to build, design the right architecture, and bring it to life with live demos and proofs-of-concept — guiding teams from first conversation to production.

    This role is ideal for someone who loves to build, is energized by talking with other engineers, and takes pride in turning a hard technical problem into something that just works. Real-time voice and video is visceral — latency, quality, and reliability are felt, not read about — so the best conversations include something live. You'll collaborate closely with our Sales, Engineering, Product teams to win technical decisions and to make sure what you hear in the field informs how we build.

    love to build and solve the most challenging customer problems with LiveKit.

    have a curious mind with a continuous desire to learn and improve.

    enjoy demoing and presenting, whether to a room or engineer, to a CTO or at a conference.

    have a team first mentality, seeking to lift others around you as you progress in your career.

    Partner with an account executive as the technical lead on strategic deals — from discovery and architecture design through demos, POCs, and technical decisions.

    Advise customers on cloud architecture and deployment across self-hosted and LiveKit Cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure).

    Build live demos and reference applications — voice agents, video pipelines, telephony integrations — tailored to each customer's use case, and reusable by the wider team.

    Scope and run proofs-of-concept against clear, shared success criteria, guiding customers all the way to production.

    Reason with customers about connectivity, infrastructure, and end-to-end latency to design for scale and reliability.

    Create technical content — blog posts, guides, webinars, and conference talks — that helps developers and enterprises build with LiveKit.

    Act as the technical enabler for your region's pod, and share field insight with Product and Engineering to help shape the roadmap.

    4+ years in solutions architecture, sales engineering, or a customer-facing engineering role (or equivalent hands-on engineering experience with strong customer instincts).

    Hands-on experience with at least one major cloud provider (AWS, GCP, or Azure) — you can architect, deploy, and debug real applications.

    Comfortable with the modern deployment toolchain: containers, Kubernetes, infrastructure-as-code, and networking fundamentals (load balancing, DNS, firewalls/NAT).

    Able to reason about connectivity, infrastructure, and latency end to end — how architecture, network path, compute, co-location, and model choice shape the AI agentic experiences of today.

    Strong programming ability in at least one of our core SDK languages — Python, TypeScript/Node, or Go.

    A clear communicator who can demo, present, and write for technical audiences.

    Working knowledge of real-time media protocols and their latency/quality trade-offs (WebRTC, RTP/SRTP, WebSockets).

    Familiarity with the AI voice stack: STT/TTS providers, LLM integration, speech-to-speech models, turn detection, and telephony/SIP.

    Experience speaking at meetups or conferences, or a track record of technical writing or open-source contributions.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    • You own a segment, and you run it like a growth marketer.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that uscreen is the video monetization platform for businesses building recurring revenue from video content. Our customers replace a patchwork stack of separate hosting, community, courses, email, and app vendors with one branded experience across web, mobile, and TV.

    Industry observers note that the platform is only half of it. We believe growth requires behavior, not just software. Customers don't stall because a feature is missing. They stall because they priced wrong, never built an email list, or launched an offer nobody wanted. Coaching is how we fix that, and it's part of the product rather than an add-on.

    You own a segment, and you run it like a growth marketer.

    According to recent reports, we have a cohort of smaller video businesses where retention is not where it should be. Nobody owns it today. You will. The revenue that stays in that segment, and the revenue that grows inside it, is yours.

    It has been revealed that this is a coaching role for someone with a growth marketer's mindset. We wouldn't hire a demand gen marketer who couldn't analyze the state of the business and figure out what's needed, and we won't hire a coach who can't either. You'll look at a customer's business the way an owner would: where the revenue comes from, where it leaks, and what to do next. You pull your own numbers to get there. When a customer needs a custom report to answer a growth question, you build it yourself.

    Recent findings suggest that it's a one-to-many job. Your cohort is larger than a 1:1 book, so the work is designing coaching that scales: cohort programs, group sessions, office hours, and triggered outreach when the data states a business is drifting. You'll build that motion rather than inherit it.

    Success is measured in dollars: gross revenue retention in your cohort first, expansion second. Not tickets closed, not calls booked.

    Industry observers note that A coach with a growth marketer's mindset. Maybe you've run growth or demand gen for a small business, built your own audience, or coached founders through their numbers. You understand how a membership business makes money, you pull your own analytics to see what's working, and you're comfortable doing it in front of a client. What matters is that you can find the real constraint in a business, then sit with the operator and say the honest thing.

    Industry observers note that benefits may vary depending on location and local regulations. Final eligibility and coverage details will be shared during the hiring process.
